Sibling of the narrowed-union match-capture entry (BUGS.md#match-capture-union-subject) -- same root, different sink; toolchain-caught, not silent. **The POINTER-variant flavor reaches this same decl sink**, so the split between the two entries is which SINK, not which variant form: `tmp: A | B = B(3)` then `other = tmp` narrows `tmp` to `B` off its initializer and emits `B other = std::move(tmp);` against a `std::variant<A*, B*>` -- g++ `conversion from 'std::variant<A*, B*>' to non-scalar type 'B' requested`. Reading the narrowed local DIRECTLY is fine (`(*std::get<B*>(tmp)).y`) and the isinstance route is fine (it has an extraction alias `__v`), so the local-to-local bind is the whole gap. Reproducers `/tmp/agents/probe_union_narrowlocal.py` (value variant) and `/tmp/agents/unionalias/main.py` (pointer variant). Workaround: re-annotate the local (`v: Int32 | Float64 = x`) or avoid the member-typed re-read. Fix shape: an assign-narrowed union name read at a member-typed sink must extract (`std::get<M>`) like the isinstance-narrowed sites do -- or sema should not narrow across a variant storage boundary it cannot render. NB the THIR F4 U1 gate rejects any narrowing-divergent union read (`_union_binding_divergent`), so THIR neither routes nor mirrors the shape -- verified for both faces (the pointer-variant repro falls back with `stmt.var_decl:name.union_binding_divergent`). Surfaced by the THIR F4 U1 probes. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `Send[Own[T]] | None` is not recognized as an owned (movable) param.** The `Send`/`Sync` marker distributes *inside* the Optional at construction (`Optional[Send[Own[T]]]`, not `Send[Optional[Own[T]]]`), so the owned-param peel `unwrap_optional_own(unwrap_readonly(unwrap_send_sync(ptype)))` sees `Send[Own[T]]` where it expects a bare `OwnType` and returns None -> the param is bound as a borrow instead of moved (a silent copy for a copyable T; a hard C++ error for `@nocopy`). Pre-existing (identical before the marker-peel fix; that fix covers bare `Send[Own[T]]` but not the Optional-wrapped shape). `tpy.thread.spawn`'s param is never Optional, so V1 is unaffected. Fix shape: either peel the marker per-Optional-member, or float the marker outside the Optional so the existing peel reaches it. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `Send[Own[ConcreteClass]]` param annotation fails at parse time with "not Send".** `def f(x: Send[Own[Box]])` where `Box` is a user class (even a Send-able one) raises `Parse error: 'Send[Own[Box]]': 'Own[Box]' is not Send`. Only the type-param form `Send[Own[T]]` (deferred to Phase-2) and the `@dynamic`-protocol form `Send[Own[Pet]]` are accepted; a concrete class is Send-checked too early (at parse, before the class's Send-ness is known). Workaround: use a bare `Own[Box]` param, or a generic `Send[Own[T]]`. Rejection-of-valid-code. Surfaced building the `tpy.thread.spawn` regression tests. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A tuple-typed parameter reassignment is not rejected by sema (unlike a record-typed param), so it emits an assignment against a `const std::tuple<...>&` param -> hard C++ error.** `def f(t: tuple[Int32, Int32], t2: tuple[Int32, Int32]): t = t2` emits `t = t2;` where `t` is a `const std::tuple<...>&` parameter, which g++ rejects (assignment to a read-only reference). A record-typed param reassignment is correctly rejected at sema ("Cannot reassign parameter 'x' of type 'Inner'"), but the tuple-typed param (and, presumably, other by-const-ref value aggregates) misses that diagnostic. Toolchain-caught (won't compile), not silent. Pre-existing on `master` -- reproduces without `--thir-codegen`; a pure AST/sema gap, not a THIR issue (the THIR value-scalar tuple subscript-read cell emits byte-identical broken text to the AST path). Workaround: assign to a fresh local instead of the param. Fix shape: extend the "cannot reassign parameter" sema check to tuple-typed (and other by-const-ref) value params, not just record params. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model) of the THIR tuple subscript-read cell. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A bare `str` (view) argument doesn't auto-coerce into a `bool | str` (or other view-member union) parameter -- needs an explicit `String(...)`.** Calling `f(s)` where `f(verify: bool | str)` and `s` is a `str`/`StrView` fails the C++ build: `invalid initialization of reference of type 'const std::variant<bool, std::string>&' from expression of type 'const std::string_view'`. The view isn't wrapped to the union's owned `std::string` member at the call site. Workaround: `f(String(s))` (owned) compiles. Works once the value is already a `bool | str`-typed local (e.g. a reassignable `verify` local in curl.py), so the gap is specifically a fresh view -> union-param coercion. Same view->owned family as other union-member coercion gaps. Reproducer: `_ssl_context_for(CA_PATH)` in `tplib/requests_verify_context` (worked around with `String(CA_PATH)`). Toolchain-caught, not silent. Surfaced building the Increment 5 verify-context test. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The clang-repl JIT backend (`--cxx clang-repl`, opt-in) cannot use modules needing runtime impls or managed third-party libs.** The default CompileBackend now compiles and links the session's build deps (runtime impl sources like os_impl.cpp, bundled third-party sources like PCRE2/Hinnant date, raw link flags) per eval, but the JIT backend has no link step to feed them into -- `import os` / `import re` / `from datetime import datetime` fail with unresolved symbols at JIT time. It accepts and ignores the `ReplBuildDeps` param (documented at the `execute` override). Fix shape: compile the support set to a shared object and load it into the interpreter (clang-repl `%lib`), or emit a clean "unsupported in the JIT backend, use the default backend" diagnostic when deps are non-empty. Split from the fixed CompileBackend link gap by `/tpy-fix-bug` (fix-repl-managed-libs). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] `--mbedtls=bundled` via the CMake-emit path (`tpyc -o`) fails to link `mbedtls_shim.c` and `cacert_data.c`.** The vendored `runtime/cpp/third_party/mbedtls/CMakeLists.txt` shim (generated by `scripts/vendor_mbedtls.py`) globs only `library/*.c`, so the TPy-owned glue `runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/mbedtls_shim.c` and the CA-bundle blob `runtime/cpp/third_party/cacert/cacert_data.c` are never compiled in CMake mode -> undefined references to `tpy_tls_*` / `tpy_cacert_pem` at link. The direct-compile path (default; what `tpy file.py`, `tpyc -b`, and the test suite use) compiles both via `tpyc/build/mbedtls.py::_source_files` and works. Pre-existing for `mbedtls_shim.c` (since ssl Increment 2); the CA-bundle change adds a second file into the same untested CMake blind spot. Untested (no case exercises `tpyc -o` CMake emit with a managed lib). `--date=bundled` (datetime v2) has the same gap for `runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/date_shim.cpp` -> undefined reference to `tpy::stdlib::datetime::local_utc_offset_seconds` (the vendored `tz.cpp` itself DOES build in CMake mode via the upstream `CMakeLists.txt` + `BUILD_TZ_LIB=ON` -- only the TPy-owned shim is missed). Fix shape: the CMake-emit wiring must compile the shim + bundled extra sources too -- ideally reuse the same source list `_source_files` returns so the two build paths can't drift. Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of the bundled CA store; date face added by the datetime v2 review. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] The else/elif arm of an `isinstance(x, str)` check on a `bool | str` union is not narrowed to `bool` -- `elif not x:` passes sema but emits `!(variant)` (hard C++ error).** `def f(verify: bool | str): if isinstance(verify, str): ... elif not verify: ...` -- sema accepts the elif arm's truthiness read, but codegen emits `(!(verify))` against `const std::variant<bool, std::string>&` -> g++ "no match for operator!". The RETURN-shaped sibling narrows correctly: `if isinstance(verify, str): return ...` followed by `if not verify:` compiles (the after-return continuation is narrowed; `_ssl_context_for` in tplib/requests relies on it), so the gap is specifically the elif/else-branch narrowing of an isinstance on a 2-member union. Two acceptable fix shapes: narrow the else/elif arm to the non-matched member (bool), or emit union truthiness (CPython accepts `not <union>`) -- either unblocks the shape. Loud (toolchain-caught), not silent. Workaround: restructure to isinstance + early return (what `_pool_key` in tplib/requests does). Surfaced building the Session connection-pool key. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (parity) Duplicate `Content-Length` response headers make `http.client` fall back to connection-close framing instead of using the length.** Two `Content-Length: 5` headers -> `HTTPResponse.getheader("content-length")` joins them `"5, 5"` (the documented duplicate-join), which `_digits_to_int` can't parse (-1) -> body framing degrades to read-until-EOF. CPython's `email.message` keeps a usable value and frames by Content-Length, so on a keep-alive connection TPy would read past the body / block where CPython stops at N bytes. Malformed-server-only (a conformant server sends one Content-Length). Fix shape: in `_init_framing`, take the first value of a comma-joined Content-Length (or reject per RFC 7230 6.3.2), rather than feeding the joined string to `_digits_to_int`. Surfaced by /tpy-review of http.client. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A view arg passed to an owned exception-constructor param isn't view->owned-wrapped, unlike an owned arg.** `raise UnknownProtocol(ver)` where `ver` is a `str` VIEW (a `list[str]` element / `split()` result) fails the C++ build ("no known conversion from `string_view` to `const std::string&`"); the same raise with an OWNED `str` (a `decode()` result) compiles, because owned binds the `const std::string&` ctor param directly. Workaround: `raise Ctor(String(ver))` (used in `http.client._read_status`). Same root family as the `String.encode()` gap (below) and the tuple-unpacked-view-local-seeding-owned-accumulator gap -- each a different codegen sink (concat-result method, owned-local init, exception-ctor arg) where the view->owned init wrap codegen applies to owned-param slots but not that position. Fix shape: apply the view->owned wrap at exception-constructor arg positions -- ideally fix the family at one chokepoint, not as separate narrow patches (per CLAUDE.md bug-fix discipline). Surfaced building `http.client`'s `UnknownProtocol` raise. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `.encode()` is missing on `String` (the owned string-concatenation result), though present on `str`/`StrView`.** `("a" + b).encode()` fails with "Cannot call method 'encode' on type String", but `s: str = "a" + b; s.encode()` (binding the concat to a `str`-typed local first) works, as does encoding a `list[str]` element -- so str->bytes from a freshly concatenated value needs an extra binding hop. Loud reject-valid, no miscompile; trivial workaround. Affects building byte payloads by concatenation (worked around in `http.client._build_request`, which accumulates `ln.encode()` over `list[str]` elements). Fix shape: expose `encode()` on `String`'s method surface, mirroring `str`/`StrView`. Surfaced building `http.client`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `print(v)` / `str(v)` of a recursive-union (JSON-like) value holding a top-level string prints the repr form (quoted) instead of the str form.** `type V = int | str | list[V]; s: V = "hi"; print(s)` outputs `'hi'`, CPython outputs `hi`. The recursive-union wrapper struct's `__str__`/`operator<<` delegates each member through the repr path, so a top-level `str` member is quoted as if nested in a container. Uniform across all rendering paths (`operator<<`, f-string, and `print`/`str` via `::tpy::__str__`) -- pre-existing, not introduced by the union-print fix. Plain (non-recursive) unions are unaffected: `x: int | str = "hi"; print(x)` correctly outputs `hi`. Silent wrong output (only for the top-level-string member; nested strings are correctly repr'd in both). Fix shape: the recursive-union wrapper's `__str__` should dispatch members through the str path (member `__str__`), not repr -- only the top-level rendering differs (container-nested members stay repr per Python). Surfaced fixing the bare-union print/str gap. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (parity) ASCII-only case/`is*` string methods give wrong results for Latin-1 (U+0080..U+00FF).** `upper`/`lower`/`capitalize`/`title`/`swapcase` and `isalpha`/`isupper`/`islower`/... only fold/classify ASCII: e.g. U+00E9 (small e-acute) is left unchanged by `.upper()` where CPython yields U+00C9, and `.isalpha()` on it is False vs CPython True -- silent wrong output for non-ASCII. Documented as ASCII-only in `docs/STRING_HANDLING.md`. Folded into the string-width/Unicode work: the fix is part of making `str` code-point-correct (`docs/STRING_WIDTH_DESIGN.md`), not worth a standalone patch ahead of that pass. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` (string-width design).
- **[LOW small] A jagged list literal WRAPPED in a tuple/dict in a ternary / `and` / `or` branch is rejected ("Incompatible types in ternary expression"), unlike the same wrapped literal as a list element or dict value.** `(1, [2, 3]) if c else (4, [5, 6, 7])` rejects what CPython accepts. The BARE different-size case (`[1, 2] if c else [3, 4, 5]`, `xs or [4, 5]`) already works -- a top-level pending-list branch is forced to `vector` by the `needs_list_type` path (`collect_pending_source_types`), so both branches share one C++ type. The gap is only the WRAPPED case: `collect_pending_source_types` collects top-level pending lists, not ones nested in a tuple/dict, and the ternary/logical common-type uses a separate `_ternary_common_type` / `_logical_op_result_type` path (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py`) that normalizes pending containers to concrete types and compares with `==` (keeping size) rather than routing through `unify_literal_types`. Loud reject-valid, no miscompile. Fix shape: route the pending-container case of both functions through `unify_literal_types(left, right, on_pending_pair=self.compat._demote_pending_pair)` so the same demotion that converges list/dict siblings also converges ternary/logical branches; mind the existing `needs_list_type` forcing so they don't conflict. Surfaced finishing the jagged-nested-list generalization. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A list of tuples of differing arity (`[(1, 2), (3, 4, 5)]`) is rejected as mixed types, though CPython accepts it.** The sibling tuple types `tuple[Int32, Int32]` and `tuple[Int32, Int32, Int32]` don't unify (different arity), so the list literal has no common element type. Distinct from the jagged-list class (this is about tuple arity, not pending-list size) -- a heterogeneous tuple list would need a variant/union element type to represent. Loud reject-valid, no miscompile. Fix shape: a feature -- infer `list[tuple[...] | tuple[...]]` (a union element) for mixed-arity tuple peers, as the error message already hints. Surfaced surveying adjacent shapes for the jagged-nested-list generalization. Needs `/tpy-add-feature`.
- **[MED small] An `isinstance`-narrowed union local read across a `yield` INSIDE a loop emits the `std::get` extraction twice in the same resume-case scope (`conflicting declaration 'auto& __t'`).** `def gen(t: A | B): if isinstance(t, A): for n in t.items: yield n` -- the narrowed `t` (a frame-resident `variant<A,B>`) is carried into the for-loop's resume state, where the narrowing alias `auto& __t = std::get<A>((*t))` is emitted both at the resume-case top (restoring the alias for resumed code) and inline before the yield, in the same `case S_JOIN_N: {...}` block -> g++ redeclaration. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/bottomup/dup_extract.py`. Exposed by (not caused by) the frame_slot-unwrap fix: before it, this shape failed earlier at `std::get`-against-`frame_slot`, so the double-emit was unreachable. Distinct from the simple narrow+yield+continue shape (no loop carrying the narrowed var across the suspension), which compiles -- so `os.walk` bottomup's union stack is unaffected. Loud (toolchain-caught), not silent. Fix shape: the resume-restoration of an isinstance-narrowed alias must not re-declare a name already extracted inline in the same scope (dedup the per-scope alias, or skip the inline extraction when the resume case already restored it). Surfaced building the `isinstance_union_frame` regression test. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] Direct tuple-unpack of an rvalue tuple whose elements are reference types miscompiles (`to_pointer_form: cannot take the address of an rvalue`).** `a, b, c, d = stack.pop()` where the popped tuple is `tuple[str, list[str], list[str], bool]` (reference-type `list` elements) -> g++ static_assert in `format.hpp` `to_pointer_form`. Binding the rvalue to a named local first and then unpacking or indexing (`t = stack.pop(); a, b, c, d = t` / `t[0]`) works -- so it is specifically the unpack of a *temporary* (rvalue) tuple with reference elements, where an unpacked element binds as a borrow into a tuple that is not materialized to a named local. The value-tuple case (`(str, bool)`) unpacks fine. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/bottomup/b7.py` (`a,b,c,d = stack.pop()`). Loud (toolchain-caught), not silent. Workaround: bind the rvalue to a named local before unpacking. Surfaced exploring the stack-element representation for `os.walk` bottomup. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (parity) `print(e)` / `str(e)` on a statically-typed USER exception subclass renders `<ClassName object at 0x...>` instead of the message.** Both `except ssl.SSLError as e: print(e)` (a stdlib `OSError` subclass) and `class NotFound(KeyError): ...; except NotFound as e: print(e)` (a user subclass) print the object-default form: codegen emits a `print_object_default` `operator<<` for every user record, including exception subclasses, and the static type selects it over the inherited `tpy::BaseException` message-printing `operator<<` / `__str__`. Catching the SAME raise via a BUILTIN base (`except OSError as e` / `except KeyError as e`) prints the message correctly (the base's friend `operator<<` applies). CPython prints the message in both cases (and `KeyError.__str__` additionally repr-quotes the arg -- `'msg'` -- part of the same `__str__`-fidelity family). Silent wrong output, cosmetic; tests should match exception TYPE, not `str(e)` text. Fix shape: skip the `print_object_default` `operator<<` for records inheriting a Throwable/exception base and route `__str__`/f-string/print dispatch to the inherited rendering (virtual, or a forwarding `__str__` when the user class defines none). Pre-existing (visible in committed ssl.hpp snapshots); surfaced re-probing exception text during the CPython-exact OSError feature and probing `ZoneInfoNotFoundError(KeyError)` for datetime v4. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A non-unpack tuple loop variable whose element tuple holds a reference type fails the C++ build in a resumable frame, with no TPy diagnostic.** `def walk(xs: list[tuple[Int32, Box]]) -> Iterator[Int32]: for t in xs: yield t[0]; yield t[1].v` -- the frame field is the borrow form `std::tuple<int32_t, Box*> t;` (via `has_pointer_repr_element`), but the loop advance assigns `t = ::tpy::unwrap_ref(*(*__for_r_0));` whose type is `std::tuple<int, Box>`, so g++ reports `no match for 'operator='`. Reproduces on BOTH for-strategies with the simplest possible shape -- no `Own`, no protocol, no readonly: `list[tuple[Int32, Box]]` (`begin_end`) and `Iterable[tuple[Int32, Box]]` (`iter_next`). Loud, rejects-valid. Distinct from the borrow-tuple *param*-element alias entry, which is a different site. Pre-existing and independent of the loop-var storage-form work: that change routes every TupleType element AWAY from the source-derived field (`elem_is_known_value` is True for TupleType), so the tuple path is byte-identical to before it. Fix shape: the advance must lift the storage-form element into the borrow-form field (`tuple_to_pointer`) exactly as the tuple-unpack sibling does, rather than assigning it raw. Repro `/tmp/agents/prereq/tupelem.py`. Surfaced by the merge-master semantic check on the loop-var storage-form branch. **Same defect at a second site:** a tuple LITERAL decl in a generator body -- `def g() -> Iterator[Int32]: t = (A(1), 2); yield use_pair(t)` for `tuple[A, Int32]` -- declares the frame field borrow form (`std::tuple<A*, int32_t> t;`) and assigns the storage literal `std::tuple<A, int32_t>{A(1), 2}` into it, so g++ reports the same `no match for 'operator='`. Both sites need the storage->borrow lift at the WRITE; fix them together. Repro `/tmp/agents/thir-lt/p1.py`; surfaced by a THIR fence pin whose stated premise ("an owning pointer-repr tuple frame local is STORAGE_TUPLE in codegen") the emitted frame field contradicts. **Status 2026-09-08 (verified on master):** the loop-var site now rejects cleanly at THIR (`res.loop_var`, a compile error naming the construct); the literal site still fails the C++ build. **Analysis carried over from an abandoned AST-path fix, to redo as THIR lowering arms:** ownership of a tuple-literal frame local is decided PER ELEMENT by sema's `elem_capture` -- a VALUE-captured element (fresh rvalue: `A(1)`, an `Own[T]`-returning call) is storage the frame must OWN (a borrow-form field would dangle once the statement ends), an lvalue element is a borrow the frame must POINT AT so the caller's later mutation stays visible (`t = (a, 2); yield t[0].v; a.v = 99; yield t[0].v` must print `1 99`). An all-fresh literal can take a whole-tuple owning field; a MIXED literal (`t = (A(1), a)`, either order) needs element-wise frame payload rendering -- own the VALUE-captured indices, point at the rest -- since no whole-tuple form fits (`MIXED_TUPLE_SLOT` exists but is gated on a DECLARED `Own` element, which a literal's inferred type never carries). A MIXED-ARM TERNARY element (`t = (a if cond else Box(99), 2)`) is VALUE-captured yet may pick the lvalue arm, so owning it silently COPIES (`1 1` where CPython prints `1 42`): decline it loudly, or extend the bare-local `_warn_ternary_ref_copy` to tuple-literal elements, never own it without an acknowledgment spelling. The frame-loop-var half is the same storage->borrow lift the tuple-unpack sibling already does.
- **[LOW small] (latent, believed unreachable today) A resumable frame whose loop var aliases a TEMPORARY iterable holds a pointer into its own sibling field, which the frame's move does not retarget.** When the `iter_next` source is a temporary (`for p in make_bag(): ...`), codegen stores it by value in `__for_src_N` and the loop var's borrow points *into that same struct*: `frame_slot<for_elem_next_t<Bag>> p` (a `Point*`) aliasing `frame_slot<Bag> __for_src_0`. `frame_slot<T&>`'s move copies the raw pointer verbatim, so relocating the frame after the loop var has been bound leaves the new instance pointing at the old one's storage. Introduced by the loop-var storage-form fix: before it, `iter_next` never aliased, so this self-reference could not arise. Same family as the already-filed hoisted-rvalue-temp and generator-captures-self entries. Reachability NOT demonstrated: rebinding the generator to another local is a pointer copy (no relocation), passing it to a generic consumer binds by reference, and the one path that does emit `std::move(g)` -- an `Own[T]`-taking generic record ctor -- currently fails to compile for an unrelated reason (`T` infers to the bare protocol type, producing a field of concept type, which the equivalent explicit annotation is correctly rejected for). So this is filed to be found later rather than fixed now: fixing that generic-field gap could turn this live without anyone connecting the two. Fix shape: either retarget the alias on frame move (needs the frame to know which field it points into -- awkward), or keep a temporary source out of the aliasing path by treating a self-referential `__for_src_N` element as owned. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model) of the loop-var storage-form branch.
- **[MED small] (harness, data loss) A TRANSIENT case failure during `--update-snapshots` DELETES that case's committed `expected/output.txt` and `expected/.fingerprints`.** Observed on a full `update_snapshots.py` run (which force-execs the whole corpus in parallel): 14 cases failed to build under the resulting load, and for two unrelated async cases -- `async/async_bind_cross_module`, `async/async_with_as_borrow` -- the run removed their `output.txt` and `.fingerprints`. Both cases were fine: re-run individually they build and print byte-identical output, so nothing about them had changed. The update path treats "produced no output this run" as "this case has no expected output" rather than as a failure to leave alone, so a build race silently discards the runtime-output oracle. Dangerous because the follow-up signal is weak: on a later plain run the case compares against a missing file, which reads as an ordinary snapshot mismatch, and for a `no_cpython` case nothing else would ever catch the loss. Only the `git diff` review before committing surfaced it here. Fix shape: never delete an existing `output.txt`/`.fingerprints` for a case whose build or run FAILED during the update -- only rewrite on a clean produce, and report the skipped cases. Surfaced regenerating snapshots for the loop-var storage-form unification. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (harness) A compile error in a STDLIB module surfaces as a pytest INTERNALERROR (SemanticError escaping the xdist plugin) instead of a clean per-case failure.** Seen when lib/tpy/zoneinfo.py briefly had a return-by-reference error during datetime v4.1: `update_snapshots` recorded diag.txt cleanly (per-case comp path), but the plain `pytest -k` run crashed with `INTERNALERROR> tpyc.diagnostics.SemanticError: Cannot return local or temporary...` -- the shared stdlib .o cache builder (conftest) compiles the stdlib outside the per-case diagnostics collection and lets the exception escape. Only reachable while the stdlib itself is broken (a dev-loop annoyance, not a user bug). Fix shape: wrap the conftest stdlib-cache build in a try that converts compiler diagnostics into a pytest-level error message naming the stdlib module. Surfaced by datetime v4.1 (zoneinfo available_timezones). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A discarded constructor call with a single identifier argument emits C++'s most vexing parse -- `Ctor(name);` is a DECLARATION of `name`, and -Werror=parentheses fails the build.** `ZoneInfo(key)` as a bare expression statement (constructing only for the raise-or-not side effect, discarding the value) emits `::tpystd::datetime::ZoneInfo(key);`, which C++ parses as a parenthesized declaration of a variable `key` -> "unnecessary parentheses in declaration" under -Werror. Loud, not silent. Workaround: bind the result (`z = ZoneInfo(key)`). Fix shape: emit discarded ctor-call statements as `(void)Ctor(arg);` or `{Ctor(arg);}`-brace form. Surfaced by datetime v4's zoneinfo error tests. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A container PARAM or an UNANNOTATED container local in an f-string is rejected ("cannot be used in f-string"), though an annotated container local renders fine.** `def f(xs: list[Int32]) -> str: return f"{xs}"` errors `Type Ref[list[Int32]] cannot be used in f-string (no __str__ or __repr__ method)`; same for `xs = [1, 2]; f"{xs}"` (errors on `PendingList[...]`). The ANNOTATED-local form `xs: list[Int32] = [1, 2]; f"{xs}"` compiles and renders via `::tpy::list_to_str(xs)` -- so the renderability machinery exists and only the type-shape unwrap is missing: `_analyze_fstring` (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py`) checks `container_to_str_template(resolved)` after peeling readonly/Own but not the `Ref[...]` param wrapper nor pending container types (`PendingList`/`PendingDict`/`PendingSet`). Loud reject-valid, no miscompile. Workaround: bind to an annotated local first (copies a param's container). Fix shape: extend the unwrap chain at that one check (Ref + resolve-pending), mirroring how print's arg path resolves the same shapes. Surfaced writing the THIR F6 S2 (f-string) eligibility tests. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (parity) `print(e)` on a caught exception binding prints the object repr, not `str(e)`.** `try: raise E("hi") except E as e: print(e)` prints `<E object at 0x...>` in TPy but `hi` in CPython (`print` calls `str`, which routes through the exception's `__str__`/`message`). `str(e)` directly DOES give `hi` -- so the message is stored and `__str__` works; it's `print()` of an exception-typed value that fails to dispatch through `__str__` (it falls to the default object repr). Pre-existing, orthogonal to interop (surfaced writing the user-exc `@export` boundary tests, which dodge it by routing parity through real CPython and not printing caught bindings on the TPy side). Affects any `print(caught_exc)`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` (print/`__str__` dispatch for reference/exception-typed args).
- **[LOW small] A list literal mixing a str-family LOCAL (pending-str or `String`) with a str literal is rejected as "mixed types", with a degenerate message.** `v = "vv"; ys = [v, "c"]` errors `List literal has mixed types: element 2 is str, but earlier elements are str. Use a type annotation like list[str | str]` -- the two "different" types PRINT identically because a pending-str local and a str literal are the same family but fail element unification. Same for a `String` concat element: `[p + q, "z"]` -> `list[String | str]`. A str PARAM element (`[p, "c"]` with `p: str`) unifies fine, and the ANNOTATED form (`ys: list[str] = [v, "c"]`) compiles and correctly wraps the view element (`{std::string(v), "c"}`) -- so the machinery exists; only literal-element unification misses the str-family peers (PendingStr/StrView/String vs LiteralType[str]). **No str literal is needed to trigger it:** two PENDING-str peers fail the same way, because each carries its own `var_id` and so compares unequal to its sibling -- `x, y = src` then `xs = [x, y]` (both unpack targets, `tuple[str, str]` source) gives the same degenerate `str` vs `str` message. That sub-shape is the more common one, since CLAUDE.md style prefers the unannotated local; reproducer `/tmp/agents/pendview/r8_listinf.py`. Any fix must unify pending-str peers with EACH OTHER, not only against literals. Loud reject-valid, no miscompile; trivial workaround (annotate the local). Reproducers `/tmp/agents/probe_s5_bug2.py`, `/tmp/agents/probe_s5_bug3.py`. Fix shape: unify str-family peers to owned `str` in list/set/dict-literal element unification (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py`, the "mixed types" check), mirroring how the annotated path resolves the element slot; the error message should also render distinguishable type names when it does fire. Surfaced probing the THIR F6 S5 (container-of-str) cell. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (rejects valid code, loud) A module-level `def print(...)` shadowing the builtin turns every `print(...)` call site into a hard compile error.** `def print(x: Int32) -> None: return` then `print(5)` errors `in function 'main': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (expr.call:call.builtin_special)`; drop the shadow and the same file compiles. `_is_builtin_print` (`tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py:13712`) correctly declines a shadowed `print` -- a same-module function/record of that name, or a local -- and the builtin print-stream arm (`tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py:14482`) is the only thing that lowers a `print` call, so the shadowed call falls through to the special-builtin gate (`tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py:3707`, `fi.qualified_name in _SPECIAL_BUILTIN_QNAMES or e.func_name == "print"`) and is refused. CPython calls the user's `print`. The old symptom was silent wrong output (the emitter intercepted `print` unconditionally, ignoring the shadow); the failure is now loud, so what remains is an unusable shape rather than a parity divergence. Exotic -- shadowing `print` is rare, and the internal-alpha audience makes it lower value than everyday rejections. Fix shape: route a shadowed `print` through ordinary function resolution instead of the builtin gate. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] The polymorphic-slicing guard over-rejects a polymorphic borrow passed to a `Callable[[Base], ...]` parameter, because `CallableType` param types skip the `RefType`-wrap ordinary params get.** `def f(cb: Callable[[OSError], None]): ...; cb(e)` where `e` is a caught (possibly-subclass) `OSError` is rejected by `_check_polymorphic_slicing` (`tpyc/sema/compatibility.py:250`) with "cannot store 'OSError' borrow as owned 'OSError' in argument ... (slicing)". But the guard is WRONG here: it returns early for `RefType`/`ReadonlyType` targets and only fires on a *bare* polymorphic `NominalType`; ordinary reference-type params are `make_ref`-wrapped before the guard sees them (and emit `const Base&`), but `CallableType.param_types` are stored raw, so the guard sees a bare `OSError` and treats the call as an owned store. Codegen would actually emit the callable param as `OSError&` (`_callable_param_cpp`: non-value -> `T&`), which binds a polymorphic borrow with NO slicing -- proven by the regular-param analogue `def handle(e: OSError)` which compiles, accepts a caught exception, and emits `const OSError&`. CONSEQUENCE: a plain `Callable[[OSError], None]` callback (the CPython-natural spelling) is rejected; users must annotate the callback param `readonly[OSError]` (which makes the target a `ReadonlyType` -> guard returns early -> emits `const OSError&`). This is what forces `os.walk`'s `onerror` param to be `Callable[[readonly[OSError]], None]` -- a workaround for THIS bug, not a real divergence (CPython needs no annotation). When the symptom is a named-function arg (not a lambda) the fall-through error is the unhelpful "'<name>' is not a variable" rather than anything about slicing/readonly. **Fix shape:** `RefType`-wrap (or otherwise treat as by-ref) `CallableType` param types before the slicing guard checks an argument against them -- a callable param slot is by-reference, never an owned store. Once fixed, drop the `readonly` from `os.walk`'s `onerror` (and any other `Callable[[exc], ...]` slot) so plain/lambda callbacks need no annotation. Surfaced + root-caused verifying the os.walk onerror `readonly` requirement. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] (perf) `key in self.<dict-field>` inside a `__contains__` method body emits O(n) `std::ranges::contains` instead of O(1) `.contains()`.** Precise trigger (bisected): membership whose RHS is a `self`-attribute, evaluated *inside a method named `__contains__`*, misses the `resolved_contains` fast path (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py:1187`), so lowering falls to the ranges arm (`binop.set_ranges_membership`, `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:3890`), which `tpyc/thir/emit.py:1738` prints as `std::ranges::contains(this->_store, k)`. The **identical** body in any other method (`def other(self, k): return k in self._store`), or membership on a local/param dict inside `__contains__` (`k in some_local`), resolves to `.contains()`. So it is NOT a return-vs-`if`-context split (both contexts emit `.contains()` normally) and NOT value-type-dependent -- it is specifically self-attr membership within `__contains__`. Looks like an over-broad self-recursion guard: suppressing self-RHS contains-resolution inside `__contains__` (to stop `x in self` recursing) but wrongly catching `x in self.<dict-field>`, where the target's `__contains__` is the dict's, not the enclosing class's. The exact suppression site is not a single obvious guard line -- needs an Explore pass over the membership / `resolved_contains` resolution in sema, which is where the fact is DECIDED. Correctness-equivalent (the probe builds and prints the right answers, just linearly); immaterial for small dicts (HTTP headers) but a cliff for large ones. Fix shape: scope the guard to "RHS resolves to the SAME class whose `__contains__` is being analyzed" rather than "RHS involves `self`". Surfaced by `CaseInsensitiveDict.__contains__` in `tplib.requests`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` + Explore survey.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud) `@overload __init__` on a user-defined class makes EVERY construction of that class a hard compile error -- `this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (expr.call)`.** `class Point: @overload def __init__(self, v: Int32): ... @overload def __init__(self, v: str): ...` plus an implementation: both `Point(1)` and `Point("hi")` are refused at the call site, while dropping the two `@overload` stubs and keeping the same `v: Int32 | str` implementation compiles -- so the overload GROUP is the trigger, not the union param. `_ctor_shape_ok` in `tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py` bails on `if len(overloads) != 1: return False`, and the ctor arm of `_lower_expr` in `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py` raises `ThirUnsupported(call_reject_reason("expr.call"))`. This supersedes the older accepted-then-silently-dropped symptom (only the first overload's ctor was emitted and a call matching the second failed against the first's signature): the parity hazard is gone and the gap is now plain missing support. Registration still accumulates the stubs; user-record ctor resolution and emission consult a single `__init__`. Methods and free functions DO support overloads; ctors are the gap. Builtin-stub ctor overloads (the exception family) work via per-overload `@native(function=True)`/`@cpp_template`, a different path. Fix shape: either wire user-record ctor resolution + codegen through the same overload-group machinery methods use (emit one C++ ctor per overload body), or reject `@overload __init__` on user records in sema with a diagnostic that names overloads. NB a full symmetric-ctor-overloads implementation was built and then reverted; it had no stdlib user once `timedelta` float ctor args were dropped. Consequence today: user OSError subclasses (`SocketError`, `gaierror`, the requests tree) keep a single `(errno, strerror)` `__init__`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` (or `/tpy-add-feature`).
- **[LOW small] A pending container LOCAL passed to an `@overload`-ed callable never matches: "No matching overload for f(PendingList[...]#N)" -- the internal type name also leaks into the message.** `ms = [5, 6, 7]; total(ms)` where `total` has `@overload` stubs taking `list[Int32]` (either arity) is rejected at overload resolution: the strict-match classifier has no pending-container arm, so a `PendingListType` arg matches no candidate (free functions and user-record ctor overload groups alike; pending-STR views DO match). Symmetric and loud, but it (a) rejects the idiomatic unannotated local the non-overloaded paths accept, and (b) prints the internal `PendingList[IntLiteral(5), 3]#0` repr in a user-facing error. Workaround: annotate the local. Also blocks witnessing the ctor-overload-group arg marks (`calls.py` `_resolve_ctor_overloads` loop, `statements.py` overloaded-raise loop) with container args. Reproducers `/tmp/agents/setbug/ovl_free_pending.py`, `ovl_pending.py`. Surfaced covering the pending-arg-marks fix's overload paths in /tpy-review. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `bytesview_to_bytes` coercion is ARG-context-blind (always copies), unlike `strview_to_str` (ARG-identity) -- an asymmetry that forces per-family special-casing at owned sinks.** At an ordinary ARG position a `bytes` param lowers to `::tpy::BytesView`, so a `BytesView` arg should be identity there (as a `StrView`->`str` arg is via `strview_to_str`'s `c == CoercionContext.ARG and not OwnType -> e` branch, `tpyc/coercions.py:377`); but `bytesview_to_bytes` (`tpyc/coercions.py:441`) emits `::tpy::bytes_copy(e)` regardless of context -- its codegen lambda ignores the context param entirely -- so a bytes view arg arrives already-owned. Consequence: the varargs-element view->owned sink, `_lower_vararg_pack` (`tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:12715`), splits its str/bytes element arm by family -- the STR leg peels the identity coerce and wraps a BORROW-form read in the owned copy (`vararg.view_elem_copy`), while the BYTES leg lowers UNPEELED and lands bare (`vararg.bytes_elem`), because wrapping would double-copy `bytes_copy(bytes_copy(bv))`. Fix shape: add the ARG-identity branch to `bytesview_to_bytes` matching `strview_to_str`; then the varargs sink can route BOTH families through the single BORROW-form wrap and drop the bytes leg (so this fix and that leg are coupled -- update both together). A cleaner long-term home for the "does this coercion already own?" question is a `produces_owned_copy` field on `Coercion`. Verify no bytes-param call site relied on the eager copy (a `bytes` param is a borrow/span, so identity should be sound) before flipping. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness, architecture-fit) of the varargs view->owned fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] The simple-generator peephole runs post-yield code BEFORE delivering the yielded value (observable ordering divergence from CPython).** A simple generator (single yield in a tail for-over-iterable / while loop) with a statement AFTER the yield -- `for x in xs: yield x; print("resume", x)` -- consumed in a for-loop prints `resume` BEFORE the consumer sees the value: TPy emits `resume:1 / got:1`, CPython `got:1 / resume:1`. The `make_generator` lambda computes the yield value, runs the post-yield body, then returns -- so the post-yield code executes within the same `__next__` call that should have already suspended. General (reproduces with `Int32`, `/tmp/agents/walk/p_yieldcross_int.py`); the resumable path orders correctly (`/tmp/agents/walk/p_yc_resumable.py`), so forcing such generators off the peephole (a post-yield non-control statement disqualifier, like the existing post-yield break/continue one) is the likely fix shape. Pre-existing; surfaced building `os.walk`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. **DEFERRED to post-IR** -- the reroute is the right fix but is IR-entangled; see the sibling entry "the simple-generator peephole runs the body prologue eagerly..." for the full analysis (the disqualifier can't be made sound + non-regressing pre-IR; it rides the THIR/MIR migration).
- **[MED] A str/bytes view tuple-unpack target first-declared in a FOR-loop body from an owned-temp source, read after the loop, dangles (UAF).** `for i in range(n): a, b = split2(s)` then `print(b)` hoists `b` to the outer scope as `std::string_view` aliasing the per-iteration `auto __tup = split2(...)` temp, which dies each iteration -- the post-loop read is use-after-free (no TPy diagnostic; reads freed memory). Pre-existing (compiles+dangles identically at the merge-base; the tuple-unpack-hoisting fix closed the if/else + match branch variants but not this loop-body one). The branch-predecl owned-promotion (`deduction.promote_predecl_view_targets`) is NOT applied at the for-loop hoist site (`sema/expressions.py:_promote_pending_loop_var`) because a blanket promotion there would also wrongly OWN the safe leaked-loop-var case (`for k, v in pairs: ...; use(k)`, where the iteration var aliases the live container, not a temp). Telling the two apart requires source-lifetime analysis: own the target only when its source is a per-iteration owned `__tup` temp (call/owned source, `not source_binds_by_ref`), keep the view when it aliases a container element that outlives the loop. This is the same precise-escape-analysis deferred to the IR migration (TODO.md). Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/tupuaf/forbody_str_after.py`. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model, architecture-fit) of the tuple-unpack-hoisting fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] A reference-type local hoisted across an if/else, match, or try/except branch that aliases a BRANCH-LOCAL source dangles -- scalar form is a SILENT use-after-free, tuple-unpack form is a loud C++ build error.** When a reference-type (record/list/...) local is first-assigned inside both arms of a branch and read after it, codegen hoists it to the outer scope as a `T*` and assigns `name = &(source_element)` per arm. If the source is itself branch-local (declared inside the arm), the pointee dies at arm exit and the hoisted pointer dangles. (try/except is also a site, since its branch-assigned vars hoist the same way: `try: o = make(); a = o except E: o2 = make(); a = o2; a.v = ...` hoists+dangles like the if/else face -- repro `/tmp/agents/tupuaf/ref_try_branch_local.py`.) Two faces:
  - **Scalar (silent UAF):** `if c: o1 = Box(1); a = o1 else: o2 = Box(2); a = o2` then `a.v = 99; print(a.v)` -> `Box* a; ... a = &(o1); ... a = &(o2);` with `o1`/`o2` branch-local. After the branch the pointee is freed; the post-branch read is a use-after-free with no diagnostic (reads freed stack -- "works" by luck). Repro: `/tmp/agents/tupuaf/ref_scalar_branch_local.py`.
  - **Tuple-unpack (loud error):** `if c: a, b = t else: a, b = t` (`t: tuple[Box, Box]`) then `a.v = ...` -- the two arms emit inconsistent forms: the is_new arm aliases (`a = &(unwrap_ref(tuple_elem_ref(std::get<0>(__tup))))`), the is_new=False arm takes the rvalue rebind-slot path (`a = &*(__slot = ...)`, `__slot` a `std::optional<Box>`) -> g++ "no known conversion from Box* to optional<Box>". The codegen asymmetry makes tuple fail to compile rather than silently dangle. Repros: `/tmp/agents/tupuaf/ref_branch_hoist.py` (durable source -- this one is actually safe to alias, see below), `/tmp/agents/tupuaf/ref_branch_local.py` (branch-local).
  
  **DURABLE-source version is correct and must stay:** when the source outlives the branch (a function-scope tuple/var, a param, the leaked for-loop var aliasing the live container), aliasing is right and matches CPython's shared mutation -- the scalar durable case already works (`/tmp/agents/tupuaf/ref_scalar_branch.py`), and the for-loop tuple case works (`/tmp/agents/tupuaf/ref_loopvar_after.py`). So the bug is specifically the BRANCH-LOCAL source; a blanket reject or blanket-own would break the durable case (owning a record also breaks the shared-mutation aliasing CPython has). **CPython note:** CPython survives the branch-local case because the binding keeps the object alive (refcounting); TPy's inline/stack records have no such keep-alive, so the branch-local target would need to *own* (move the element out of the dying source), while the durable target must *alias*. **Root cause:** reference-local hoist-across-branch aliases its source with no check that the source outlives the hoist scope. **Fix shape:** source-lifetime / escape analysis -- alias when the source outlives the target's hoist scope, own (move out) when it does not; this is the reference-type sibling of the str/bytes Option-B over-own item in TODO.md (same analysis, different remedy: str/bytes can conservatively own since a copy is observationally identical, reference types cannot). A conservative sema rejection of branch-local-sourced reference hoists is a possible interim but was deferred (it over-rejects the durable case and is inconsistent with the silently-compiling scalar form). Surfaced by /tpy-fix-bug of the (former) tuple-only S1; the scalar silent-UAF face was found during that analysis. Needs the escape-analysis work (IR) for the precise fix.
- **[LOW small] Single-member union narrowing's post-fall-through extraction matches members by `==`, so a cross-module same-short-name member may not match.** `_narrows_to_union_member` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py:1767`) and the plan builder beside it (`_post_if_narrow_plan`, same file, `any(m == member for m in u.members)`) check membership with `TpyType.__eq__`. If the narrowed fact and the declared member differ in a way `==` doesn't bridge (two cross-module records sharing a short name), the extraction is skipped and the "variant has no member" g++ build error appears -- a loud failure, not a silent miscompile. **Re-check and withdraw:** the generic-alias half was probed 2026-09-03 -- `def f(v: list[int] | str)` with `if isinstance(v, str): return 0` then `len(v)`, run through `tpyc --dump-code` -- and the extraction fires correctly (`auto& __v = *std::get<std::vector<::tpy::BigInt>*>(v);`), so a generic alias IS bridged by `==`. Only the cross-module same-short-name half remains untried; if that also matches, delete this entry. Fix shape if it does reproduce: match members by the same nominal/qname identity rule sema uses elsewhere (`same_nominal_symbol_loose`) rather than raw `==`. Surfaced by /tpy-review of `fix-union-else-narrowing`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `os.strerror` uses non-thread-safe `std::strerror`.** `tpy::stdlib::os::strerror` (`runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/os_impl.cpp`) wraps `std::strerror`, which on some POSIX platforms returns a pointer into a shared static buffer -- a data race if `os.strerror` is called concurrently from multiple threads. glibc 2.32+ (the primary Linux target) is thread-safe, and CPython's `os.strerror` carries the same property, so this is latent hardening rather than an active bug. Fix shape: use `strerror_r` with a caller-supplied buffer. Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp-correctness) of the os process/system batch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (rejects valid code, loud) A module-global value-Optional (`str | None` / `bytes | None`) cannot be narrowed with `is not None` at all.** `text: str | None = "hi"` then `if text is not None:` errors `stmt.if:if.cond_binop.is not.optional_other_nonetype:binop.shape.is not` in a plain function and `res.cond:binop.shape.is not` inside a generator/coroutine, so the for-loop the shape was filed for is never reached. `_lower_binop`'s `_IS_OPS` arm (`tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py:3608-3623`) rejects unless one of `_is_none_compare_operand` / `_any_none_subject` / `_opt_record_none_subject` / the mixed-tuple ptr-element row recognizes the operand, and a global-slot read of a value-Optional is recognized by none of them. Tightly scoped (both probed): a module-global `Int32 | None` narrows fine, and a function-local or param `str | None` narrows fine -- it is the GLOBAL + value-Optional pair specifically. Worth queueing: a module-level optional string is ordinary Python. This supersedes the older silent form of the entry -- the resumable for-source used to build its iterator from the raw global access with the optional deref missing, a wrong runtime result with no diagnostic; that emitter is gone, so the failure is loud instead. Fix shape: teach `_is_none_compare_operand` the global-slot value-Optional read, then confirm the resumable for-source over the narrowed global applies the global-slot + optional deref. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] `os.path.realpath` can return a *relative* path when `std::filesystem::absolute()` fails.** `path_realpath` (`runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/os_impl.cpp`) does `abs = absolute(input, ec); if (ec) abs = input;` then `weakly_canonical(abs, ec)` with an `abs.lexically_normal()` fallback. If `absolute()` errors (a pathological cwd -- e.g. the cwd was removed), `abs` stays the un-absolutized relative input and the result can be relative, violating realpath's always-absolute guarantee (CPython joins cwd unconditionally). Rare; no TPy diagnostic. Fix shape: on `absolute()` failure, join `current_path()` manually rather than falling back to the raw input. Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp-correctness) of os.path.realpath. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] `os.path.expanduser` `~user` silently drops the home dir if the passwd entry exceeds the getpw buffer (ERANGE not retried).** `current_home`/`user_home` (`runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/os_impl.cpp`) size the `getpwuid_r`/`getpwnam_r` buffer from `sysconf(_SC_GETPW_R_SIZE_MAX)` (fallback 16384) and treat *any* non-zero return -- including `ERANGE` -- as "not found", returning `""` (-> expanduser leaves `~user` verbatim). A passwd entry larger than the buffer is misreported as a missing user rather than retried with a grown buffer. Practically unreachable (16384 covers real entries); robustness only. Fix shape: loop doubling the buffer on `ERANGE`. Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp-correctness) of the pwd binding. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] `os.environ` snapshot build reads `extern char** environ` without synchronization.** `environ_keys()` (`runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/os_impl.cpp`) walks `::environ`; a concurrent `setenv`/`unsetenv` (which may reallocate the array) is a data race per POSIX. NOT currently reachable -- the snapshot is built once at program startup, before any user thread runs -- so this is a latent hazard only if snapshot construction is ever moved off the startup path. No fix needed today; noted so a future change doesn't reintroduce a live race. Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp-correctness).
- **[MED] An `@overload` method on a type imported from another module does not resolve at the call site (`No matching overload`).** A free function with `@overload` stubs resolves correctly across module boundaries, but the same overload set on a *method* does not: calling `inst.get(k)` where `inst`'s type (with an overloaded `get`) is defined in a different module fails with `No matching overload for 'get' with argument types (...)`, even for an arity/type that matches a stub exactly. Same class, same method, same call -- defined and called in *one* module resolves fine; split across modules fails. Confirmed with a 2-module repro (`/tmp/agents/osenv/pkg/{leaf,main}.py`: an `M` with `get(key)->str|None` / `get(key,default)->str` overloads, `inst=M()` in `leaf`, `inst.get("a")` in `main`). Likely the overload group (keyed by `id(first_impl)` in `analyzer.overload_groups`) is registered per-analyzing-module and not carried across the module registry for imported types, so the downstream module sees only one stub (or none) when resolving the call. Workaround: collapse the method to a single non-overloaded signature (e.g. `os.environ.get` is `get(key, default=None) -> str|None`, the `dict.get` shape, instead of the typeshed str / str|None overload pair). Surfaced building `os.environ` (the `_Environ.get` accessor, always called from a downstream user module). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] `timedelta` day-overflow `OverflowError` message predates CPython 3.12.** `timedelta(days=10**9)` correctly raises `OverflowError` at the range check (`if d < -_MAXORDINAL_DAYS or d > _MAXORDINAL_DAYS` in `lib/tpy/datetime.py timedelta.__init__`), but the message is the old CPython `"timedelta # of days is too large"` vs 3.12's `"days=N; must have magnitude <= 999999999"`. Message-only divergence (the guard itself is correct -- an earlier "accepts-invalid" symptom was an artifact of a since-reverted two-overload ctor, not the current single ctor). Pre-existing. Align the message to 3.12 if a datetime parity pass revisits it.
- **[LOW small] Not every type-mismatch formatter routes through `disambiguated_pair`, so a same-short-name cross-module collision still renders unqualified at the un-converted sites.** `qualify-mismatch-diagnostics` + `fix-mismatch-diag-nested` route the main `expected X, got Y` sites (top-level + element/key/value) and the list-literal/comprehension element formatters through `disambiguated_pair`, qualifying nested leaves (`list[red.Tag]`) via the `_qualify_nominals_in_str` flag. Remaining gaps: (a) ~5 `expected {expected}, got {actual}` sites in `tpyc/sema/compatibility.py` (~1080/1091/1247/1258/1310) still interpolate bare `str()`; (b) the dict-key and set literal-element formatters in `tpyc/sema/expressions.py` only fire under a union/optional-guarded branch, so a plain `s: set[red.Tag] = {blue_tag}` collision routes elsewhere unqualified; (c) the union-vs-member shape (`Tag | int` param vs a narrowed `Tag` arg -> `expected Tag | int, got Tag`) is not a same-string collision so `disambiguated_pair` never fires. The rejection is correct in every case; only the label is ambiguous (rare cross-module same-name pairing). **Fix shape:** route the remaining `compatibility.py`/`expressions.py` formatters through `disambiguated_pair`; while consolidating, give `qualified_type_str`/`disambiguated_pair` a shared diagnostic-render home (a `sema/diagnostics.py` / `type_render` module rather than `typesys.py`) and let `NominalType.__str__` short-circuit on `_module_qname` before the `is_user_record` registry lookup. Surfaced by /tpy-review of `fix-mismatch-diag-nested`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The two type-to-C++ rendering paths use different cross-module identity rules, a latent re-collision seam.** `NominalType.to_cpp` keys `native_cpp_names` by short name (`self.name`) with a qname-keyed lookup only as a *preference*; codegen's `TypeResolver.type_to_cpp` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/types.py`) is qname-aware via `imported_record_qualification_for_type`. `fix-cross-module-type-identity` made the qname path authoritative almost everywhere (and added qname keys to `native_cpp_names` so `to_cpp` disambiguates same-short-name records), but the two paths still look interchangeable while resolving identity differently. Any future emit site that reaches C++ via `to_cpp` for a type whose qname key was *not* registered (e.g. a record reachable only through a path that doesn't populate the qname key) would fall back to the short-name `native_cpp_names` entry and silently reintroduce the B114 same-name collision class. The specific sync point is record registration in `tpyc/codegen_cpp/generator.py` (the per-emit-module `native_cpp_names` population): a new record-registration path that sets the short-name key but forgets the canonical-qname key degrades silently, with no tripwire unless a same-short-name cross-module pair happens to exist in the program -- the most likely regression vector. No active miscompile today (the union/record/constructor paths are already qname-direct); this is a structural hazard. **Fix shape:** make `to_cpp` resolve the cross-module C++ name from the record's qname (mirroring `type_to_cpp` / `error_return_to_cpp`) rather than a short-name map with a qname fallback -- ideally collapsing the two paths. THIR is the natural home (see `docs/IR_DESIGN.md` Open Questions item 13). Surfaced by the `fix-cross-module-type-identity` retrospective. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `is_return_exception` / `register_return_exception` still identify `ReturnException` types by bare short name: any user class sharing a registered exception's short name is treated as a `ReturnException`.** `register_return_exception` (`tpyc/typesys.py`) stores `record.name` and `is_return_exception` strips its (already-qualified) input back to a bare name before a compilation-global set lookup, so e.g. a user class named `StopIteration`, or a second `JsonError` colliding with `tplib.json`'s, is wrongly classified return-only. The *propagation*-matching half of this cluster (`error_return_matches` conflating two distinct same-short-name exceptions, the C++-build-error symptom) was fixed in `fix-error-return-identity` by comparing the full defining-module qnames. Keying the set by qname is **blocked on a re-export-canonicalization decision**: `StopIteration` is *defined* in `tpy._builtins._exceptions` but registered/looked-up as the public `builtins.StopIteration` (the `__next__` form at `methods.py` and the builtins-preference in `qualify_exception_name` both produce the public qname, while registering from the defining module would produce the private one), so naive qname-keying breaks `StopIteration` recognition (generators/iterators). **Fix shape:** decide whether the canonical identity of a re-exported builtin exception is its defining-module or its public (`builtins`) qname, make `qualify_exception_name` and the set-registration agree on that one form, then key `return_exception_names` (and `BUILTIN_RETURN_EXCEPTIONS`) by it; or replace the bare-name cache with a protocol-implementation check that consults the resolved record (the cache exists only to bridge the pre-`_exceptions`-compiled ordering). Audit finding B113 (residual half). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` or `/tpy-add-feature` (the canonicalization decision).
- **[LOW] `os.stat` nanosecond timestamps overflow (signed UB) past year ~2262.** `tpy::stdlib::os::ts_ns` (`runtime/cpp/src/stdlib/os_impl.cpp`) computes `static_cast<int64_t>(tv_sec) * 1000000000LL + tv_nsec`; for `tv_sec` beyond ~9.2e9 (year 2262) the multiply overflows a signed `int64_t` -- UB the compiler may exploit. The float-seconds fields (`st_mtime` etc.) are unaffected. Benign in practice, but the multiply should saturate or use an unsigned intermediate. Surfaced by /tpy-review (runtime-cpp-correctness) of os stat. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `float`/`Float32` arithmetic with `bool` is rejected (`3.0 + True`), though CPython treats `bool` as an `int`.** The float operators widen over the `AnyFixedInt` marker protocol (every fixed-width int extends it), but `bool` does not extend `AnyFixedInt`, so `float OP bool` finds no overload ("Invalid operand types"). Rejects-valid, not a miscompile; workaround is an explicit cast (`3.0 + Int32(True)` or `3.0 + int(b)`). Fix shape: either add a `bool` (or a shared `AnyFixedInt`-including-`bool`) overload to the float/Float32 arithmetic dunders, or treat `bool` as conforming where fixed-width ints do. Surfaced by /tpy-review (docs-sync) of the float-fixed-int-arith fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] Subscript-assign / del on a class with `__setitem__`/`__delitem__` but no `__getitem__` is rejected at sema ("Cannot index type ... no `__getitem__`").** CPython allows a write-only / del-only mapping (`m[k] = v` / `del m[k]` need only `__setitem__`/`__delitem__`, not `__getitem__`), but TPy's subscript sema requires `__getitem__` even on the assign/del target path. Workaround: add a `__getitem__`. Surfaced fixing the write-subscript non-int-key dispatch (the inverse-test class needed a `__getitem__` it shouldn't have). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED medium, deferred: MIR] A `match` capture of an `A | B` (union) subject fails the C++ build -- two distinct sub-causes (spiked).** [`match-capture-union-subject`] The pointer-repr **Optional**-subject half was fixed in `fix-match-capture-indirect-subject` (the capture aliases the pointer directly); the union half remains and is **bigger than a codegen tweak**. (a) **Narrowed union**: `x: A | B = A(1); match x: case q:` -- the assignment narrows `x` to `A`, so the match analyzes as a *record-A* match (q typed `A*`), but `x`'s storage is the pointer-variant `std::variant<A*,B*>` -> `cannot convert std::variant<A*,B*>* to A*`. A narrowing-type-vs-storage-form mismatch. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/c3probe/mu.py`. (b) **Genuine union**: `def m(x: A | B): match x: case q:` -- `q` is hoisted in storage form (value-variant `std::variant<A,B>`) but the subject is borrow form (pointer-variant `std::variant<A*,B*>`) -> `no match for operator=`. This is the **borrow/storage-form duality for union captures** (the IR-gated class, IR_DESIGN OQ9): q must either be hoisted in borrow form (pointer-variant, aliasing the subject) or the bind must convert (`to_value_variant`). Reproducer `/tmp/agents/rev2/union_param.py`. The aliasing form for a union capture is a **design decision** (pointer-variant alias vs value-variant copy-out vs per-variant narrowing), so this is `/tpy-add-feature` (design) more than `/tpy-fix-bug`, and the form half is best sequenced with THIR. Workaround: narrow with `isinstance` per variant before mutating. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the audit-#11 work; root causes spiked.
- **[LOW small] A walrus aliasing a reference-type loop element assigns a `const T*` into a non-const `T*` local -- ill-formed C++, no TPy diagnostic.** `for x in items: if (y := x).v > 1:` over a `list[Node]` emits `const auto& x = *__beg_0;` next to `Node* y = nullptr;`, then `(y = &(x), *y)` -- g++ "invalid conversion from 'const Node*' to 'Node*'". It reproduces in a plain for loop as well as the comprehension form this entry was filed from (`result = [y for x in items if (y := x).v > 1]`), so the fault is the walrus BINDING, not the comprehension. The originally-filed symptom -- a borrow pointer pushed into the storage-form result container -- is GONE: the comprehension element read now derefs (`__result.push_back((*y));`, with the usual "copies Node into owned storage" warning). Site: the `expr.walrus_ptr_alias` arm of `_lower_expr` in `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py` sets `is_const = borrow_decls[e.target]` and prefixes `const` on the predecl from it; `borrow_decls` is sema's `function_stmt_borrow_decls` (assembled in `tpyc/sema/analyzer.py`), which leaves the target non-const even though the loop element binds `const auto&`. Toolchain-caught (hard C++ error), not silent. Workaround: none inside a comprehension; in a loop, read the field directly instead of binding it. Fix shape: make the walrus predecl inherit the const-ness of its borrow SOURCE (a read-only loop element), or bind the loop element non-const when a walrus aliases it. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] Generic constructor/function inference cannot bind a type parameter to a `readonly[T]` type.** When the only evidence points to a readonly binding -- an expected type of `Own[Rc[readonly[T]]]` and/or a `Ptr[readonly[T]]` argument against a `Ptr[T_param]` parameter -- inference produces no binding and raises `Cannot infer type arguments for '<Record>'`, even though `<Record>[readonly[T]]` is the obvious solution. Confirmed (DIAG) on the `@auto_readonly` const overload of `Rc.clone`: hint `Own[Rc[readonly[T]]]`, args `['Ptr[_RcCellBase]', 'Ptr[readonly[T]]']`, yet inference fails; the mutable overload (no readonly) infers fine. Root cause is the readonly-stripping in arg/seed handling (`_restore_readonly_arg` / `seed_subst_from_record_pattern` in `tpyc/sema/calls.py`) erasing readonly before the type param is bound, plus no path to bind a param *to* a readonly type. Worked around in interior-mutable fields by spelling the construction type explicitly (`Rc[auto_readonly[T]](...)`, transformed per-overload by `@auto_readonly`); if this inference gap is fixed, that explicit marker can be dropped in favor of plain `Rc(...)` inference. Surfaced building the interior-mutable / readonly-`Rc.clone` feature. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, perf] `key in <readonly dict>` emits a linear `std::ranges::contains` scan instead of the O(1) `.contains` hash lookup.** A membership test on a `readonly[dict[K,V]]` (e.g. `key in self._data` inside a `@readonly`/auto-readonly method) lowers to `std::ranges::contains(this->_data, key)` -- O(n) over the keys -- rather than the dict's O(1) `__contains__`. Root: the membership sema path resolves `__contains__` via `get_record_for_type(right_type)` without unwrapping `ReadonlyType`, so the dict's `contains` is not found and it falls back to the generic iterable scan (the readonly-dict-reads fix made `in` *work* on a readonly dict, via the iterability path, but not via the O(1) accessor). Mutable-dict `in` is O(1); only the readonly receiver degrades. Correctness is fine; perf only. Fix: unwrap `ReadonlyType` at the membership `__contains__` lookup (one site). Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness) of `collections.Counter`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, deferred: MIR] `collections.Counter.most_common` fails the C++ build for a REFERENCE-type key.** Its `sorted(pairs, key=lambda kv: -kv[1])` over a `list[tuple[T, int]]` is the stdlib witness of the key-lambda param-form entry further down: the lambda param is rendered `const std::tuple<val_or_ptr_t<T>, BigInt>&` (borrow form) while `builtin_sorted_key` calls it with the vector's storage element `std::tuple<T, BigInt>`. VERIFIED distinct from the tuple-literal slot selection and reproducible with a CONCRETE key type (`sorted(pairs, key=...)` over a `list[tuple[Item, Int32]]` emits `[](const std::tuple<Item*, int32_t>& kv)`), so it is not a generics artifact. Latent for Counter itself because every current `Hashable` is a value type. Fix is the same one item 9 gates -- see the `key=` lambda entry below; kept here only so a search for `Counter.most_common` lands somewhere. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` (IR-gated).
- **[LOW small] The `Hashable` C++ concept requires only `__hash__`, but membership (`std::ranges::contains` / `__contains__`) needs `==`.** A user type that satisfies TPy `Hashable` (defines `__hash__`) but not `Equatable` (no `__eq__`) compiles as a dict key / Counter key but fails the C++ build at the membership/contains site. Python's `Hashable` does not formally imply `__eq__` either, but a hashable-without-`__eq__` type is degenerate; the gap is that TPy accepts it as a key then fails late in C++ rather than rejecting at sema (dict key validation should require `Hashable` AND `Equatable`). Pre-existing protocol gap, exposed by `collections.Counter`'s `T: Hashable` `__contains__`. **Other end of the split recorded in the `[T: Hashable]` dict-LITERAL entry near the top of this file**: that literal-site gate (`validate_hashable_container_elem`) demands Hashable AND Equatable and so over-rejects a bounded `T`, while this annotation path demands neither and under-rejects a concrete key. Different trigger and opposite failure mode -- not duplicates -- but one consistent key-validation rule closes both; fix them together. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A generator method that iterates `for k in self._data` AND subscripts `self._data[k]` with the loop var emits ill-formed C++.** The frame-hoisted loop var binds `k = &(*((*__for_it_0))++)` as mutable `T*`, but iterating a dict yields `const T*` -> g++ "invalid conversion from `const std::string*` to `std::string*`". A yield-only generator (`for k in self._data: yield k`) compiles fine; adding any `self._data[k]` subscript inside the generator triggers it (the loop var must be bound `const T*` in the frame). Blocks the natural `collections.Counter.elements()` (`for k in self._data: while j < self._data[k]: yield k`). No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error only. Workaround: build an eager `list[T]` in a non-generator method instead of a lazy generator. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/gen_dict_sub.py`. Surfaced building `collections.Counter`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] Subscript-assignment through a FIELD-access target rejects a readonly-sourced key, while the same through a bare-name target works.** Inside a readonly method, `result._data[copy(k)] = self._data[k]` (where `k` iterates the readonly `self._data`, and `result` is a fresh local of a dict-wrapping class) fails sema with "Cannot pass readonly[T] as mutable T in dict key (expected T)"; the identical pattern with a bare `dict[T,int]` local target (`out[copy(k)] = self._data[k]`) compiles. So the subscript-assignment key check for a field-access target (`obj._data[key] = v`) does not unwrap/accept the key the way the bare-name-target path does (the readonly-dict read fix covered the READ subscript + bare-target paths, not the field-access assignment target). Blocks `collections.Counter`'s `+`/`-`/`&`/`|` operators (they build a fresh `result` Counter and write keys into `result._data`). No miscompile -- sema rejection. Workaround: route writes through a method whose receiver is mutable. Reproducers: `/tmp/agents/ctr_add.py` (fails) vs `/tmp/agents/iso27.py` (bare-target, works). Surfaced building `collections.Counter`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid, loud) An `and`/`or` whose result type is `bool` but with a RECORD operand is a hard compile error.** Two triggers, both refused: (a) two unrelated record types, `if dogs[0] or cats[0]:` -> `(stmt.if:if.cond_binop.||.record_f1_record_f1:truthy.shape)`; (b) a record `or` a non-record, `if a or 0:` -> `(stmt.if:if.cond_binop.||.record_f1_other_intliteraltype:truthy.literal)`. This supersedes the older symptom (the bool-result path emitted the raw C++ `a || 0` and g++ answered "no match for 'operator||'"): the mis-render no longer has an emitter, so the shape is refused instead of miscompiled. Site: `_lower_truthy` in `tpyc/thir/lower/expressions.py` -- `raise ThirUnsupported("truthy.literal")` on a literal operand, `raise ThirUnsupported("truthy.shape")` on the residual-shape tail. Both rejects reach well past the record family this entry was filed for: `if a or 0:` with a plain `a: Int32` is refused the same way (`scalar_other_intliteraltype:truthy.literal`), and a bare `if dogs[0]:` with no logical op is refused as `stmt.if:cond.subscript` -- everyday shapes, so the queueing case is stronger than the record-only headline suggests. The value-result path (same-type / `__bool__` records returning the operand) still routes. Fix shape: give the literal and record/subscript operands their truthiness renders in the bool-result path (the conversion the value-result path already applies), rather than leaving the tail as a reject. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] Nested-def sema isolation deep-copies the whole per-function tracking state, so type objects (and every other identity-bearing structure in it) come back as CLONES after a nested def statement.** `scope_tracker.nested_def_scope` snapshots via `save_function_state` (a `deepcopy`) and restores the copy; `current_scope`/`current_ns` identity is now explicitly re-attached (fixing frame-local hoisting after a nested def -- bindings landed in the cloned ns while `_collect_generator_locals` read the original), but other deep-copied fields (`narrowed_types`, borrow tracker state, write history) still hold cloned `TpyType` objects post-def -- any consumer keying on type identity (`is`, `id()`-keyed tables) across a nested-def statement can silently mismatch. No observed miscompile; latent hazard. Fix shape: replace the blanket deepcopy with an explicit save/restore of the fields nested-def analysis actually mutates (or a shallow copy-on-write layer). Surfaced while making nested defs frame members. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] Mutation of a CAPTURED name via a call with mapped arguments inside a nested def is still lost -- only the direct-mark and self-receiver channels replay.** The nested-def mutation-fact replay carries direct marks (field writes, structural mutations, not-known-readonly method calls) and `receiver_is_self` call edges; edges that carry mutation through argument positions do not survive: a `MutationCallEdge` whose `param_map` indexes the nested def's own params is dropped (the indices don't translate to the enclosing function), and `helper(self)` / `helper(xs)` with a CAPTURED arg records no param entry at all (the `self -> -1` sentinel and the caller-index map are installed only for the enclosing function's own params, not for captures -- `_prescan_and_analyze_body` is method-body-gated). So `def fill(xs): def go(): helper(xs)` (or `helper(self)`) where `helper` mutates its param under-marks -> the enclosing param/method emits `const` and the C++ build fails at the mutation site (loud, no silent miscompile). Fix shape: capture-aware edges (a per-callee "captured name -> callee param idx" map on the nested def's FunctionInfo, resolved in the Phase-2 fixpoint). Surfaced implementing the nested-def self-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A nested-def PARAM (or staticmethod local) literally named `self` inside a record still renders through the receiver rule.** The codegen self-spells-this predicate (`self_renders_as_this` / `self_captures_this`) reads the ENCLOSING method's `current_func_params`, so a nested def declaring its own `self` param renders the body reference `(*this)` while the param binding is the shadowing local -- uncompilable C++ (the capture list correctly omits it). Staticmethod locals named `self` no longer capture `[this]` (the predicate requires `current_method_record_type`), but the body renderer shares the same blindness. Sema has the mirror twin: the mutation-fact replay's `replayable` set includes `"self"` unconditionally, so a nested def whose own param is named `self` inside a method replays that param's mutations onto the receiver (const-loss only, no semantic change). Degenerate shadowing shapes; loud C++ failure. Fix shape: track nested-def-scope param shadowing in the emission context (push/pop `current_func_params` per nested body). Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness) of the nested-def self-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A lambda INSIDE a nested def capturing `self` emits no capture for it -- loud C++ `'this' was not captured` error.** Inside the nested-def analysis the tracking state's `definitely_assigned` excludes `self`, so the inner lambda's capture filter (`free_names & definitely_assigned`) drops it: the emitted inner lambda has no `this` capture while its body renders `this->field`. Same blind spot family: `receiver_self_in_scope()` reads `current_function` (the nested def, `is_method` False), so the escape-mode skip and the Send by-ref pin would also miss the shape -- moot today since it never compiles. Reproducer `/tmp/agents/nested-self/lambda_in_nested.py`. Fix shape: include the receiver in the nested analysis's capturable set (and derive receiver context from the enclosing method, not `current_function`) when the enclosing method has one. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective of the nested-def self-access branch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] Borrow/consume facts other than mutation are not replayed out of nested-def analysis, and the nested def's own FunctionInfo carries no facts at all.** The nested-analysis restore discards `mark_param_returned` roots (a closure returning a borrow of `self`/captured storage), `mark_own_param_consumed`, and addr-escape names; only mutation marks and self-receiver edges replay. The nested `FunctionInfo` registered for call resolution is likewise built with no mutated/structural/return-borrow facts, so return-borrow dangle checks through closure calls are blind. Pre-existing blindness (facts were never carried), newly reachable now that self-capturing closures compile. Fix shape: stamp the nested FunctionInfo's Phase-1 facts from the nested tracking state before restore, and replay returned/consumed roots like mutation marks. Surfaced by /tpy-review (safety-model) of the nested-def self-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A `Callable`/`std::function` argument passed into an `async def`/generator is copied into the coro frame instead of moved.** `_classify_params` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_async.py`) classifies a `Callable[[...], R]` param as `VALUE` (not `FN`), so `_factory_args_forwarded` forwards it by bare name (no `std::move`); the coro-frame ctor then copy-constructs the `std::function` from the factory local. `std::function` copy is well-defined but non-trivial (potential heap alloc), so e.g. `asyncio.start_server`'s `_accept_loop` copies its `cb` once per spawn instead of moving. Pre-existing (latent until a Callable param reached an async factory); not a safety issue. Fix: forward a last-use `Callable` factory arg with `std::move`. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the async-fn->Callable coercion branch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] An async-fn ref whose param is a borrow (`T`) coerced to a callable hint whose param is `Own[T]` is accepted by sema but miscompiles -- C++ build error.** `async def handle(reader: StreamReader)` passed where `Callable[[Own[StreamReader]], Own[Cancellable[None]]]` is expected: the function-ref match unwraps both `Ref` and `Own` on param types, so `StreamReader` (borrow) is treated as compatible with `Own[StreamReader]`, but the synthesized coroutine-factory wrapper takes the hint's `Own` param as `StreamReader&&` and `std::move`s it into `handle`, whose actual param is the lvalue ref `StreamReader&` -> g++ "cannot bind non-const lvalue reference ... to an rvalue".
