The borrow form is also unsound here (the handler's frame would borrow the wrapper-lambda local, dropped when the lambda returns while the coroutine lives on). Fix: in the function-ref-to-callable match, require an `Own[T]` hint param to match an `Own[T]` (not borrow `T`) function param, with a clean sema diagnostic. Workaround: annotate the handler param `Own[T]`. Part of the async-fn->Callable coercion (`feat-async-fn-callable-coercion`); toolchain-caught. Surfaced by the `examples/net/stream_server.py` handler. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A loop-carried `Own[T]` local cannot be returned -- last-use analysis is conservative inside a loop, so `return owned_local` from within a `while`/`for` is rejected as a borrowed/non-last-use source.** A redirect-style loop that reassigns an owned local each iteration and returns it on the exit branch (`resp = fetch(...); while ...: resp = fetch(...); return resp`) fails with "Cannot return borrowed value ... The source is borrowed (parameter, attribute, or non-last-use variable)", even though the return is genuinely the last use on that path. The conservative "used inside a loop that may iterate" rule (documented in `docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` last-use section) over-fires for the return position. Workaround: express the loop as recursion (each `return` is then straight-line last-use) -- used by `tplib.requests` `Session._hop` for the redirect chain. Same last-use-precision family as the try-assigned-local entry below. **Fix shape:** treat a `return <local>` that post-dominates all of the local's in-loop reassignments as a last use (move), or defer to the MIR move-state model. Surfaced building `tplib.requests` redirect following. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A local assigned inside a `try` and moved after the `try` block is not recognized as last-use-movable -- a `@nocopy`/owned such local fails to move.** `try: conn, addr = await f() except OSError: break` then `Rc.new(conn)` after the try -> "@nocopy type 'socket' cannot be copied ... Only the original owner can be moved at its last use", even though `conn` is bound only on the non-exception path and read only after the try. The conservative "a value read on an exception path stays live across the whole try body" rule over-fires: it keeps a try-*assigned* local live across the try even when it is not read inside the try. Workaround: avoid the `try` (e.g. stop a loop via cancellation rather than catching the error), or move the binding+use entirely inside the try. Distinct from the await-tuple-unpack move (which works without the try). Surfaced building `asyncio.start_server` (catching listener-closed around `sock_accept`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A generic (templated) `async def` awaited as a sub-coroutine loses its template args in the awaiter's frame slot -- C++ build error.** An `async def`/method that is generic OR takes an `Fn`/protocol-typed param (so its coro frame is a template, `__coro_g<F>`) and is `await`ed from another coro emits `std::optional<__coro_g> __sub_N;` in the awaiter frame (no `<F>`), then `__sub_N` is "not declared in this scope" at the poll site. The sub-coro frame-slot type omits the generic frame's template arguments. Reproducer: `async def spawn(factory: Fn[[Int32], Own[Cancellable[None]]], n): asyncio.create_task(factory(n)); await asyncio.sleep(0)` then `await spawn(worker, 7)`. Distinct from the non-generic case, which monomorphizes fine. Blocks the `Fn`-template target of the async-fn-as-coroutine-factory coercion (the `Callable` type-erased target works). Toolchain-caught, not silent. Surfaced probing higher-order async for `start_server`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A concrete container passed where a GENERIC recursive-alias instance (`Tree[Int32]`) is expected is accepted by sema but fails the C++ build -- no clean diagnostic.** `type Tree[T] = T | list[Tree[T]]; def depth(t: Tree[Int32]): ...; xs = [1, 2, 3]; depth(xs)` -> g++ `invalid initialization of reference of type 'const Tree<int>&' from 'std::array<int, 3>'`. The std-container guard in `compatibility.py` `_check_compat` only catches a `UnionType`-with-wrapper element difference, not its generic sibling `RecursiveAliasInstanceType`, so `_check_union_member_type_args` accepts the element-wise coercion and codegen can't emit it. The non-generic case is rejected cleanly (a concrete container into a `UnionType` wrapper hits a diagnostic that names the workarounds); the generic sibling falls through to the raw C++ error instead. Fix shape: extend the guard's element check to fire for `RecursiveAliasInstanceType` too (and ideally cover the cross-container `Array`->`list`-member route, which the same-name guard misses). Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/deepconv/genalias.py`. Surfaced surveying recursive-union argument forms. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] Mutating a recursive-union param's nested container through a `match` binding fails the C++ build (param wrongly inferred `const`) -- CPython mutates and propagates.** `type V = Int32 | list[V]; def mutates(x: V): match x: case list() as items: items.append(1)` emits `void mutates(const V& x)` -- mutation tracking does not follow the `case list() as items` binding back to the param, so const inference marks `x` non-mutating; the match binding `items` is then `const`, and `items.append(1)` is a g++ error (`passing const ... discards qualifiers`). CPython mutates the caller's list in place (`reads(a)` 2 -> `mutates(a)` -> `reads(a)` 3). Toolchain-caught, not silent. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/deepconv/mutprobe.py`. Fix shape: mutation tracking must propagate a structural mutation of a match-arm capture alias back to the matched param (the alias is a borrow of the subject). Surfaced probing recursive-union param mutation. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A list literal does not coerce to an `Iterable[T]` (generic protocol) parameter: `f(["a", "b"])` where the param is `Iterable[T]` fails the C++ build.** `c.add_all(["a", "b"])` where `add_all(self, items: Iterable[T])` errors `no matching function ... add_all(<brace-enclosed initializer list>)`. The literal isn't materialized into a concrete `list[T]` (then matched against `Iterable[T]`) at the call boundary. Workaround: bind to a local first (`xs: list[str] = [...]; c.add_all(xs)`). Sibling of the literal-into-`Optional[list]` gap below (collection-literal contextual coercion not firing for a wrapper/protocol target). Surfaced building `collections.Counter`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] `dict.get(k, "<lit>")` with a str/bytes-literal default fails the C++ build: the literal default is not coerced to the value type `V`.** `d: dict[str, str]; d.get("k", "<none>")` -> `no matching function for call to dict_get_default(ordered_map<string,string>&, const char[2], const char[7])` -- the `"<none>"` default stays `const char*`/`const char[N]` instead of being coerced to `std::string` (the value type `V`) before the call, so template deduction fails. The named-local workaround (`fb: str = "<none>"; d.get(k, fb)`) compiles. Same family as the `d.get(k, [])` empty-collection-default entry (the `default: V` param's type doesn't flow into the literal). Surfaced fixing the dict-value narrowed-Optional bug. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A collection literal does not coerce to an `Optional` collection param: `f(["a", "b"])` where the param is `list[str] | None` fails the C++ build.** `csv.DictReader(fp, ["name", "age"])` (param `fieldnames: Own[list[str]] | None = None`) emits a brace-init `{...}` that g++ can't convert to `std::optional<std::vector<std::string>>` ("no known conversion from <brace-enclosed initializer list>"). A plain `list[str]` param takes the literal fine (`DictWriter(out, ["name","age"])` works) -- only the `| None` wrapper breaks it. Workaround: bind the literal to a local first (`fn: list[str] = [...]; DictReader(fp, fn)`). Root: the list-literal materialization targets the bare element type, not the `optional<vector>` storage, so the brace-init is ambiguous. Likely the same family as the dict/set-literal contextual-coercion gap (a plain concrete target hits the peer-unify branch); here the target is `Optional[list]`. Fix: route a collection literal whose expected type is `Optional[C]` through the same materialize-into-`C` path, then lift to the optional. Surfaced building `csv.DictReader`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] An `async def` returning a tuple built from named owned (`@nocopy`/`Own`) locals COPIES the elements instead of moving them -- C++ build error.** `async def f() -> tuple[Own[A], Own[B]]: ...; a = A(...); b = B(...); return (a, b)` emits, in the coro frame, `std::tuple<A, B>{(*a), (*b)}` from the `std::optional<A>`/`std::optional<B>` frame slots (lvalues) with no `std::move`, so g++ fails `use of deleted function A(const A&)` for a `@nocopy` element. The async-return tuple-literal path does not apply last-use move to its frame-slot element locals. Workaround (used in `asyncio.open_connection`): build the tuple from fresh rvalues inline (`return (A(...), B(...))`), which C++ move-constructs. Sync-function tuple returns and the single-element / rvalue cases work; only the async-return tuple of multiple *named* owned locals is broken. Same move-out-of-named-owned-local family as the named-source whole-tuple unpack entry below, different site (async return tuple construction). Toolchain-caught, not silent. Surfaced building the asyncio streams layer (`StreamReader`/`StreamWriter` returned from `open_connection`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `KeyError` from a missing dict key carries the message `"KeyError"` instead of the key value -- `str(e)` is `"KeyError"`, CPython's is `"'absent'"`.** A missing-key read (`d["absent"]`) raises a `KeyError` whose *type* is correct (so `except KeyError` works), but `tpy::__getitem__` for `ordered_map` (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/dunder.hpp` ~167) calls `raise_key_error("KeyError")` with a fixed string rather than the formatted key. CPython reprs the key (`KeyError: 'absent'`). One-sided: catching works, message-comparing diverges. Same shape as the documented `str(KeyError(k))` gap noted for the builtins dict surface. Fix: format the key into the message (gated on the key type being printable/repr-able). Pre-existing; surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the const-container subscript-read fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (perf) A `with ... as` target whose `__enter__` returns `StrView` gets owning frame storage but its read still carries BORROW form, so a `yield` of it copies an already-owned string.** `with_owning_str_targets` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_async.py:3291`, feeding `FrameLayoutPlan` via `_frame_layout` at `:1183`) gives the target an owning `std::string` frame field, but the yield sink `_wrap_view_owned_sink` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py:478`, called from `tpyc/thir/lower/resumable.py:2388` and `tpyc/thir/lower/simple_gen.py:490`) keys on the lowered value's Form fact, which still says BORROW for that read -- so `yield label` emits `return std::string(label);`, an owned->owned copy. Pinned by `tests/cases/generators/gen_yield_view_from_frame::with_view_target`, so a fix shows up as a snapshot delta. An `__enter__ -> str` target is NOT affected: view deduction promotes it and the read is storage form. The sibling instance -- a `str`/`bytes` PARAM copied into owned frame storage on the way in (`is_owned_in_coro_frame`) -- is already correct, pinned bare by `owned_param_stays_bare` in the same case. This one is really a SYMPTOM of the entry below (the target should not have been promoted to owning storage at all), so fixing that removes it. Fix shape: derive the read's Form fact from `FrameLayoutPlan`, the declared single source of truth for the frame-field form, since the instance is exactly "this field is owning". Note the plan's domain must be WIDENED first -- `_frame_layout` classifies `func.generator_locals` only, and params are classified separately (`_CoroParamKind` / the simple-generator capture list), so this is not a drop-in lookup. Pure perf (an owned string copied twice), no wrong output. Surfaced by the /tpy-merge-master check once `FrameLayoutPlan` landed.
- **[LOW small] (perf) A `with ... as` target whose `__enter__` returns a VIEW is promoted to owning frame storage on the strength of its type CATEGORY, not its provenance.** The with-prescan (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_async.py` ~2993) adds the target to `with_owning_str_targets` whenever `is_str_category(resolved_enter_t)`, and that category spans `str`, `String`, `StrView` and `FStr`. The rationale in the comment there is specifically the `__enter__ -> str` case, where the C++ signature returns `std::string` BY VALUE and a `string_view` field really would alias a temporary dying at the assignment's semicolon -- owning is required for that one. For `__enter__ -> StrView` the C++ return is already a `std::string_view`, so nothing owns, and whether a view field dangles depends on what it views: `with h as label:` where the frame holds `Holder& h` and `__enter__` returns a view of `self.label` is lifetime-stable, so the copy at `label = (*__with_ctx_0).__enter__();` buys nothing. That lifetime-stability argument holds only for a BORROWED manager, and only because the promotion covers the shape at all: an OWNED (rvalue) manager whose view target skips the promotion has nothing keeping the viewed object alive, which is why the manager is now frame-homed whenever the target's field points into it (`_with_field_points_into_manager`) -- so removing this promotion is safe for the owned case too, but only alongside that homing. Costs one owned-string copy per `__enter__`. It is also the CAUSE of the redundant yield-sink copy in the entry above: the field is owning while the read predicate still calls it a view, so the wrap fires on an already-owned string -- with a correctly-viewed field the wrap would be doing real work instead. Pinned as-is by `generators/gen_yield_view_from_frame::with_view_target`, so a fix surfaces as a snapshot delta. Fix shape: split the promotion by the enter type's C++ ownership -- keep it for the owning returns (`str` / `String`), and route a view return through the source-lifetime question `frame_unsafe_source` already answers for deduced view locals (`tpyc/sema/local_deduction.py`). Same shape-vs-provenance call, and this is the last view-family frame-storage decision still keyed on shape alone. Surfaced by user review of the yield-sink branch's with-target snapshot.
- **[LOW small] `json.dumps((1, 2, 3))` (a tuple) is rejected** -- `tuple` is not a `JsonValue` member, so a tuple argument fails the union match. CPython serializes tuples as JSON arrays. Divergence: idiomatic `json.dumps((a, b))` works in CPython. Resolving it means either adding tuple handling to `JsonValue` / `json.dumps` (tuples are heterogeneous value types -- not a clean union member) or a dedicated tuple->array coercion in the json layer. Surfaced surveying json.dumps input forms. Likely `/tpy-add-feature`.
- **[LOW small] `csv.writer(..., doublequote=False)` silently emits malformed CSV for a field containing the quotechar.** With `doublequote=False` and no escapechar, a field that needs quoting and contains the quotechar is wrapped in quotes without escaping the inner quote (`lib/tpy/csv.py` `_format_row`), producing unparseable output; CPython raises `csv.Error("need to escape, but no escapechar set")`. Only on the non-default `doublequote=False` path. Fix needs a small surface decision first: TPy `csv` has no `csv.Error` type -- either add one (matching CPython's hierarchy) or raise `ValueError`. Surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of csv v1. Needs `/tpy-add-feature` for the error-surface call, then a localized fix.
- **[LOW small] Module-qualified construction of a generic class fails: `mod.GenericClass(...)` reports "Module has no function 'GenericClass'".** `csv.DictReader(fp)` (a generic `class DictReader[W]` accessed via the module attribute) is rejected, while `from csv import DictReader; DictReader(fp)` resolves and deduces `W` correctly. Module-attribute access resolves functions and non-generic classes but not generic-class construction. Workaround: direct import. Surfaced building `csv.DictReader`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `sorted(d.items(), key=...)` (and other element-type inference) on a readonly dict fails: `items()` yields `readonly[value]` for a value-typed V.** `d.items()` on a `readonly[dict[K, int]]` is typed `dict_items[K, readonly[int]]`, so iterating yields `tuple[K, readonly[int]]`; passing it to `sorted(..., key=lambda kv: -kv[1])` makes overload/type-param inference conflict (`tuple[K, readonly[int]]` vs the lambda's `tuple[K, int]`). `readonly[int]` is pointless (a value V read from a dict view is a copy), but it is materialized eagerly by `@auto_readonly` on `items()`/`values()`. The other readonly-dict reads (`.get`, `in`, for-iteration, `d[k]` with a readonly key, readonly *reference*-value reads) now work; only `.items()`/`.values()` projecting readonly onto a VALUE element is unfixed. Workaround: build the pairs list manually (`for k in d: pairs.append((k, d[k]))`) then sort that. **Fix shape:** the collapse must be POSITION-AWARE -- `readonly[value-type]` collapses to the value type only in a value position (tuple/dict-view element), NOT under `Ptr`/`Span`/`SpanIter`/`Ref` where it is the const-pointee/element (a broad `substitute_type_params` collapse breaks `Ptr[readonly[T]]` / ReadOnlyPtr -- verified). Cleanest is making `auto_readonly` value-aware at substitution (resolve `AutoReadonlyType[V]` to bare V when V is value, `readonly[V]` when reference) rather than the eager `apply_auto_readonly`. Surfaced building `collections.Counter`'s `most_common`; deferred from the readonly-dict read-access fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A generator that takes a protocol-typed parameter cannot be embedded (iterated) inside another resumable frame.** `for row in _parse_rows(fp, ...): ...` where `_parse_rows(fp: Readable) -> Iterator[...]` is itself a generator, placed inside another generator/async body, errors: "cannot iterate '_parse_rows(...)' here: a generator with protocol-typed parameters cannot be embedded in a resumable frame yet; bind the elements first (e.g. `xs = list(...)`) and iterate those". The loud diagnostic + the `list(...)` workaround are correct, but it forces eager materialization for any lazy generator-over-generator pipeline whose inner stage has a protocol param. A generator with a *concrete* (or `Ptr[R]`) param embeds fine. Note the enclosing generator must actually be resumable for the reject to fire -- a simple-generator outer gets the lambda peephole and compiles. **Blocks lazy `csv.DictReader`** (and any pipeline of protocol-param generators). Root cause is a TYPE-SPELLING gap, not a representation gap: `_temp_iterator_field_cpp` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_generators.py`) must name the callee's frame struct as the enclosing frame's `__for_src` field type, and a protocol-param callee's struct is a template (`__gen_callee<T_items>`) whose deduced argument the embedding site does not compute. Fix shape: derive the template argument from the call site's argument type (the same deduction the factory call performs) instead of rejecting. NOTE: this is a DIFFERENT root cause from the loop-var storage-form defect once filed on this entry (fixed -- the `iter_next` for-strategy now spells the loop var's frame field from the iteration source, so C++ picks alias-vs-own); fixing one does not fix the other. Surfaced building `csv.DictReader`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (silent) A GENERIC generator hands its element out BY VALUE, so a consumer's mutation never reaches the source container.** `def bump_all[T](items: Iterable[T]) -> Iterator[T]: for it in items: yield it; yield it` over `[Point(1), Point(2)]`, with the consumer doing `p.x += 100`, leaves the list at `1 2` where CPython reads `201 202`. The generator frame's `__next__` is emitted `std::expected<T, ::tpy::StopIteration>` -- a value `T` -- where a concrete `Iterator[Point]` would yield through `val_or_ref<Point>` (borrow form). So the copy is in the YIELD slot, not the loop variable: the loop var itself is now correct for generics (a protocol-bounded `T` mutated *inside* the generator does reach the caller -- verified `101 102`), and an unbounded `T` cannot be touched inside the generator at all, which is why this only shows up through the yielded value. Distinct from the since-fixed str-view yield-slot defect (that one was loud, a `string_view`/`expected<string>` mismatch, closed by the frame view-local owned promotion); this one compiles and silently copies. Present on BOTH emit paths, and it blocks no corpus case. Re-measured 2026-09-09: the lambda peephole's generic yield slot is `std::optional<T>` and copies the same way -- a single-yield `each[T]` over `[Point(1), Point(2)]` with the consumer doing `p.x += 100` prints `1 2` where CPython prints `101 102` (`/tmp/agents/ownproto/p15_generic_yield_mutate_simple.py`), so an earlier claim here that the peephole "yields borrows correctly" was wrong; and `iterators/gen_ref_compose` (`my_map` / `my_enumerate`) builds and runs byte-identical to its committed `output.txt` with the peephole forced off (`--rebuild`, else the whole-run build cache replays the stock binary), so the claim that this entry blocked that case from surviving the peephole deletion was wrong too. Fix shape: a generic yield slot must use the same `val_or_ref`-based borrow form the concrete non-value case uses, so the element's value-vs-reference shape is settled at instantiation rather than assumed to be a value. Repro `/tmp/agents/prereq/genericelem.py`. Surfaced verifying the loop-var storage-form unification, which fixed the loop-var half and left this one standing.
- **[MED small] `async for` over a manual async iterator COPIES the iterator source into the frame, so the loop cannot mutate the object it iterates -- and a reference-typed element additionally fails the C++ build.** Two stacked defects on the `async_for` for-strategy, both reachable from one program: `class Walker: def __aiter__(self) -> "Walker": return self` + `async def __anext__(self) -> Point` iterated as `async for p in w: p.x += 100` leaves `w.items[0].x` unchanged (CPython mutates it). (1) The iterator slot is `frame_slot<aiter_type_t<Src>>` and `aiter_type_t` is `std::decay_t<...>` (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/dunder.hpp`), so a self-iterator whose `__aiter__` returns `Src&` gets *copied* into the frame at `__for_itr.emplace((it).__aiter__())` -- the loop then drives the copy. The SYNC path solved exactly this: `is_self_iterator_v` + `resumable_iter_init`/`resumable_iter_next` (`runtime/cpp/include/tpy/generator.hpp`) keep the slot empty for a self-iterator and re-read through `src`; the async path has no twin. Silent for a self-iterator, and a `@nocopy`/`Own` source would fail the build instead. (2) Independently, the `async_for` strategy never sets `pointer_form_loop_var`, so a concrete non-value element is emplaced into `frame_slot<T>` from the `T*` that `__anext__` returns -- ill-formed C++ (`invalid conversion from Point* to int32_t` inside `frame_slot::emplace`). Fixing (2) alone is a REGRESSION: it makes the program compile and silently produce the wrong answer via (1), so the two must land together, (1) first. The sibling `iter_next` strategy is already fixed for both. Async generators (`async def` + `yield`) are unsupported, so a manual `__aiter__`/`__anext__` class is the only route in. Repro `/tmp/agents/prereq/asyncfor.py`. Surfaced by the for-strategy borrow-form survey. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The for-loop result slot in a resumable frame is spelled from the ELEMENT type, so a non-value element makes it `std::expected<T&, StopIteration>` -- ill-formed C++, since a reference cannot live in `std::expected`. Two arms of `_analyze_for_strategy` do this.** (a) The `er_elem` arm: `class BagIter: @error_return(StopIteration) def __next__(self) -> Point` iterated inside a two-yield generator emits `std::expected<Point&, ::tpy::StopIteration> __for_r_0`, and libstdc++ rejects it (`non-static data member ... in a union may not have reference type` / `forming pointer to reference type`). Repro `/tmp/agents/prereq/ernext.py`. (b) The `typing.Iterator` arm for a NAMED source: same slot, same error; the temporary-source path already avoids it by spelling `decltype(std::declval<__gen_X&>().__next__())` from the stored struct rather than from the element. Arm (b) is mostly shadowed by the over-broad ephemeral-borrow rejection (a yield touching the loop var is rejected at sema first), so its reachable window is a body that mutates the element but never yields anything derived from it; arm (a) has no such shield. Loud (toolchain-caught), rejects-valid. Same borrow-form-leaked-into-an-owning-slot family as the since-fixed coro-frame `str`/view local defect, different site: there the owning slot was the yield result, here it is the `__next__` result field. Note the `er_elem` arm is also missing the borrow-form loop-var classification, but that is moot until the slot is spellable. Fix shape, covering both arms: derive the result slot from the SOURCE (its `__next__` return type, as the temporary path already does) instead of from the element type, so the borrow lands in the loop var where the storage-form classification can hold it. Was filed as two entries -- one per arm, with different prescriptions -- until the merge-master check spotted they are one defect. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A `dict`/`set` literal with a coercible-but-not-equal element type rejects-valid instead of applying the runtime-checked `BigInt -> fixed-width int` coercion.** `d: dict[str, Int32] = {"k": make_big()}` / `s: set[Int32] = {make_big()}` (where `make_big() -> int`) is rejected at sema with `Type mismatch in variable 'd': expected Int32, got int`, even though the same `int` value coerces cleanly at scalar (`x: Int32 = make_big()`) and now list/tuple-element positions (the runtime-checked `to_fixed_check`). Root: the dict/set literal analyzers' per-element contextual-coercion branch only fires when the expected element type is a union/optional/Any/recursive-wrapper/covariant-generic shape; a plain concrete target (`Int32`) falls to the `else` peer-unify branch, so the literal's type becomes `dict[str, BigInt]` / `set[BigInt]`, which the strict container-assignment element check then rejects. Distinct from the list/tuple gap that this sibling fix closed -- those *silently miscompiled* (ill-formed C++); dict/set instead *reject-valid* with a clean error, so it is lower severity. Fix shape: widen the contextual branch to any known concrete target and route plain-target elements through the same materialize-narrowing-coercion path `_analyze_array_literal` now uses (`_materialize_narrowing_element_coercion`), verifying the strict element check still rejects user-record slicing. Surfaced fixing the list/tuple aggregate-element coercion (`tests/cases/int/int_to_fixed_in_aggregate`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED medium] A protocol whose method is typed with a *same-module* recursive type alias fails the C++ build -- the protocol's concept / `@dynamic` base + `Adapter`/`RefAdapter` are emitted before the recursive-alias wrapper struct is declared.** `type Tree[T] = T | list[Tree[T]]` plus `class Counter(Protocol): def count(self, t: Tree[int]) -> Int32: ...` (or the `@dynamic` form) in one module emits, in the header, a virtual `count(Tree<BigInt>&)` / a `Counter` concept referencing `Tree<...>` *before* the same-module `template<...> struct Tree` (or its forward decl) appears -- g++ reports `'Tree' has not been declared` (structural: `concept 'Counter' not in namespace scope`; `@dynamic`: `RefAdapter` pure-virtual `count` not overridden due to the broken signature). Affects both structural and `@dynamic` protocols, generic recursive alias confirmed (non-generic recursive union likely same root, unverified). **Works cross-module**: importing the alias (`from treelib import Tree`) brings the wrapper in complete via the included header, so the ordering is satisfied -- this is the workaround. Toolchain-caught (C++ build error), not silent. Fix shape: in `codegen_cpp/generator.py` emit ordering, the recursive-union wrapper forward-decl/definition for a *local* alias must precede protocol (concept / `@dynamic` base / adapter) emission, mirroring the guarantee the imported-header path already provides. Surfaced by /tpy-ready coverage-hardening probes for generic recursive aliases (the `@dynamic`-protocol-method coverage gap). Covered cross-module by `tests/cases/protocols/dyn_recursive_alias_method`; the same-module case is the gap. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (parity) `open(dir, "r")` on a directory succeeds silently and `read()` returns `""` where CPython raises `IsADirectoryError` immediately.** `std::ifstream::open` does not fail for a directory in read mode (Linux `open(2)` with `O_RDONLY` succeeds on a directory; the failure only surfaces at `read(2)` as EISDIR, which iostreams swallow into failbit/empty), so `TextFile`/`BinaryFile`'s `is_open()` gate passes and the EISDIR arm of the errno-mapped open path is unreachable for read mode -- probe: `open("/tmp", "r").read()` prints `""` in TPy, raises `[Errno 21] Is a directory: '/tmp'` in CPython. Write-mode open on a directory DOES correctly raise `IsADirectoryError` (EISDIR at `open(2)` time). Silent divergence, and it defeats the read-mode half of the `IsADirectoryError` mapping the CPython-exact-OSError feature wired up; also blocks writing an EISDIR-through-`open()` test until fixed. Fix shape: after a successful read-mode open, `stat` the path (or attempt a zero-byte read and check EISDIR) and raise `IsADirectoryError` like CPython's `io.open` does at fd-wrap time. Pre-existing (the `is_open()` gate predates the errno mapping); surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the oserror-exact branch. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] `TextFile`/`BinaryFile` reads do not surface a genuine I/O error (badbit) -- a read that fails on a device error returns "" / b"" instead of raising `OSError`.** `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/file.hpp`: the full-read path (`read()` / `read(size<0)`) drains via `ss << fs_.rdbuf()` / `istreambuf_iterator` and never checks `fs_.bad()`; the sized-read path (`read(size>=0)`) now preserves badbit across its short-read `clear()` but still doesn't *raise* on it -- a subsequent read just returns empty. CPython raises `OSError` on a real read error. Latent: badbit on a regular file is a hardware/FS fault, near-unreachable in tests; EOF (the common short-read cause) is correctly handled as empty. Fix shape: after each read, if `fs_.bad()` (not merely `eof`/`fail`), `raise_os_error(...)` -- consistently across both the full-read and sized-read paths. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness) of the io `read(size)` change.
- **[HIGH medium] Subexpressions evaluate RIGHT-TO-LEFT, diverging from CPython's guaranteed left-to-right -- confirmed for positional call/constructor/method arguments, both operands of a binary operator, and f-string interpolations.** [`subexpression-right-to-left-eval`] Measured against CPython with a counter function `nxt()`: `three(nxt(), nxt(), nxt())` prints `3 2 1` (CPython `1 2 3`), `print(nxt() - nxt())` prints `1` (CPython `-1`), `f"{nxt()} {nxt()}"` prints `7 6` (CPython `6 7`) -- probe `/tmp/agents/dsr/r29_evalorder.py`. List/tuple literals and `print(a, b)` ARE correctly sequenced. Silent wherever the subexpressions are pure, wrong wherever they are not, and `f() - g()` needs no call syntax to trigger. Found downstream in a path tracer, where `V3(random() * 2.0 - 1.0, random() * 2.0 - 1.0, random() * 2.0 - 1.0)` drew from the random stream backwards: the result was a correctly rendered but DIFFERENT image, so nothing short of a byte comparison against CPython caught it. Raised MED -> HIGH on that evidence: the original entry was scoped to the single binary op, and the shape that actually bites -- an ordinary multi-argument call -- is both more common and equally silent. The three sub-entries below record the shapes as originally measured. **Original binary-operand measurement:** `a() + b()` (each appending to a shared list) runs `b()` then `a()` -- TPy emits the C++ expression `a() + b()` and g++ evaluates function-call arguments right-to-left (C++ leaves the order unspecified), so any observable side effect in the operands is sequenced backwards. The *result value* is correct (operator is applied to the right values); only the side-effect *order* diverges. Reproducer: `order=[]; def a(): order.append("a"); return "A"` + same for `b`; `a()+b()` gives `order==['b','a']` (CPython `['a','b']`). Notably the 3+-operand chain `a()+b()+c()` is correct (`['a','b','c']`) -- it routes through a left-to-right fold -- so the bug is specific to the single binary op. Applies to any binary operator (`+`/`-`/`*`/comparisons/etc.) whose two operands both carry side effects, not just str concat. No diagnostic; silent. Affects `<`/`==` operand order, `x[f()] = g()`-style too (unaudited). Fix shape: sequence binary-op operands left-to-right at emit (materialize the left operand into a temp before evaluating the right when either operand is non-trivial). Sequence the operands: capture the left one's VALUE before evaluating the right when either can run user code -- a reference alias is not enough, it re-reads after the write. The membership / chained-comparison sibling of this is filed above and was implemented then reverted; the two should land together so the rule is not half-applied, and the cost (a copy per affected expression) priced once for both. Probe `/tmp/agents/chain-dup/reorder.py`. Surfaced authoring the io `read(size)` tests (`fp.read(4) + "|" + fp.read()`). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`. **Same class, hoisted-arg shape:** an arg materialized as a named temp STATEMENT before the call (a ref-param rvalue -- container/record literal or call result -- to a free function, or any reference-type rvalue to a generator/coro method) evaluates before sibling inline args, so a multi-arg call mixing a hoisted arg with side-effecting inline args sequences wrong vs CPython's left-to-right (probe: `take(side("a"), [side("x"), side("y")], side("b"))` -> `x y b a`, CPython `a x y b`). Newly reachable via the resumable-method rvalue args that previously failed the C++ build. The fix shape generalizes: hoist ALL side-effecting args left-to-right once any arg hoists. **Value-typed generic slots joined the scope on 2026-09-08:** an rvalue at a generic `T` parameter used to hoist a named temp, which incidentally SERIALIZED it ahead of its sibling arguments; the temp is now taken at the instantiation, so `f(side("A"), side("B"))` at a value-typed `T` renders both inline and g++ runs B then A. Not a new class and not a reason to re-add the hoist -- the monomorphic twin always had this order, so hoisting only at the generic slot would make the generic and its twin differ (the `generic-equals-monomorphic-twin` pitfall) while leaving the twin wrong; the fix is the sequencing below, which covers both.
- **[MED small] The simple-generator peephole captures a generic `T` parameter BY REFERENCE at every instantiation, because the capture form is decided on the OPEN `T`.** [`simple-generator-captures-open-t-param-by-reference`] `_build_capture_list` (`tpyc/codegen_cpp/gen_generators.py`) captures a parameter `&name` when `ptype.is_value_type()` is False, and `TypeParamRef.is_value_type()` is False for an unbounded `T` -- so `def repeat[T](value: T, count: Int32)` emits `[&value, count, i]` even at `T = Int32`, where the monomorphic twin `def repeat(value: Int32, ...)` emits `[value, count, i]` by value. The lambda escapes (`make_generator` returns it), so a caller passing an rvalue leaves the capture referring to a temporary that dies at the end of the full expression. What keeps this sound today is the CALL SITE: an argument at a generator factory's generic slot is hoisted into a named `__tmp_N` at the enclosing statement (`_generic_arg_slot`'s `needs_temp` / `_borrowing_frame_callee`, `tpyc/thir/lower/checks.py`), whose scope outlives the statement -- eliding that temp reproduces the defect, measured as `AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-scope` reading the captured `int32_t` inside the lambda (`/tmp/agents/gu5/p_gen.py`, g++-13 `-fsanitize=address -fsanitize-address-use-after-scope`), while the hoisted render is ASAN-clean. **No suite instrument sees this**: at -O0 the dead stack slot still reads back the right value, so the comp phase, the byte-diff and the CPython comparison all pass -- the same 'tests pass by luck' shape as the `Iterable[T]`-parameter entry below, which is this defect's non-generic sibling (there the by-reference capture is CORRECT for a reference param and the escape is the fault; here the capture form itself is wrong at a value instantiation). Fix shape: decide the capture form at the INSTANTIATION rather than on the open `T` -- a value-typed `T` captures by value, matching the twin. That also removes the call-site rule that currently guards it, and with it the temp a resumable generator factory pays for nothing (see TODO.md). Same class as `generic-equals-monomorphic-twin` in `docs/PITFALLS.md`. **Sharpened 2026-09-09, when each str/bytes type got its own C++ type: the call-site temp only mitigates this while the SLOT IS A REFERENCE.** `[&value]` on a `const T&` parameter binds the TEMP; on a by-value view parameter it binds the parameter object, which dies when the factory returns. So a generator's bare-`T` param is emitted `::tpy::borrow_frame_param_t<T>` -- a reference at EVERY instantiation (mutable for a reference type, const for a value type), which is `param_val_or_ref_t`'s own formula with the two view rows bypassed -- rather than the instantiation's own parameter form, and removing that spelling reproduces the UAF as OBSERVABLE wrong output at `T = str` (`tests/cases/iterators/gen_generic` printed blank lines). It is a FORM, not a const decision: it needs no mutation fact, so a body that writes through the slot still writes through to the caller. That is the whole reason the guard's mitigation still holds, and it is what the real fix would let go of. A second face, an @overload-ed generator getting no temp at all, was CLOSED by the same unit: `_borrowing_frame_callee` reads the callee's DECLARED `typing.Iterator` return when `is_generator` is False (an overload's per-signature fi always carries False), and `_generic_root_subst` recovers the declared stub whose params are still `T`, so the generic and the overload routes now hoist identically -- `tests/cases/calls/overload_generator` passes a literal, a scalar literal and a call rvalue, and pins all three temps. Surfaced fixing the instantiated-slot argument temp 2026-09-08. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] A *simple-peephole* generator that iterates an `Iterable[T]` parameter captures the parameter by reference into its escaping `make_generator` lambda -- a dangling reference (use-after-free) once the factory returns.** `def starmap(func, it): for pair in it: yield func(pair[0], pair[1])` (a single tail-yield over the `it` param -> the simple-generator peephole, not a resumable frame) emits `inline auto starmap(__F0&& func, T_it& it) { return ::tpy::make_generator<R>([func, &it, ...]() ... { ... ::tpy::__iter__(it) ... }); }` -- the lambda captures `&it` (the reference parameter) and the returned generator outlives `starmap`, so `it` dangles. Latent UAF: it happens to read correct values when the generator is consumed immediately in the same statement (the stack slot is not yet clobbered), so tests pass by luck. The *resumable* path is unaffected -- it owns the iterable via a `T_it&&` frame field (so generators with a `break`/`continue` or a non-tail yield, e.g. `takewhile`/`filterfalse`, are safe); only the simple peephole over an `Iterable` param is wrong. No diagnostic; silent UB. **Blocks `itertools.starmap`** (reverted from v1 for this reason). Fix shape: the simple-generator peephole must own the iterable param (capture by value -- which for a reference param copies the reference to the live source -- or move it into the closure), not capture `&param`, when the generator escapes (`make_generator` always escapes). Workaround: force the resumable path (a `break`/`continue` or non-tail yield). Surfaced by /tpy-review of itertools starmap. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED, deferred: MIR] A generator holding an `Optional[T]` local across iterations and yielding a tuple of (the narrowed previous value, the current loop var) miscompiles -- the previous-value tuple element silently reads the current loop var.** `def pairwise[T](it): prev: Optional[T] = None; for x in it: (if prev is not None: yield (prev, x)); prev = copy(x)` over `[1,2,3,4]` yields `(2,2),(3,3),(4,4)` instead of `(1,2),(2,3),(3,4)` -- the `prev` element of the yielded tuple reads `x`, not the stored `prev`. Reproduces in a plain `for a, b in pairwise(...)` loop (not a comprehension artifact), so the fault is in the generator's tuple-yield of a frame-held `Optional[T]` element alongside the loop var, not the consumer. No diagnostic; silent wrong output. The single-element `Optional[T]`-across-yield path (e.g. just `yield prev`) is untested here; the miscompile is observed for the tuple-of-(prev, x) shape. **Blocks `itertools.pairwise`** (and any windowed generator that carries a previous value). Workaround: none clean (the natural formulation miscompiles). Surfaced probing itertools v2 feasibility. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A generator with a generic `Optional[T]` accumulator written across the loop fails the C++ build (`__slot_1 is not captured` / `std::optional<int>::optional(int*&)`).** `def accumulate[T](it, func): acc: Optional[T] = None; for x in it: (acc = copy(x) if acc is None else func(acc, x)); yield acc` -> g++ errors at the resumable-frame body: the `Optional[T]` accumulator frame slot is mis-emitted (a captured-temp `__slot_1` referenced out of scope, and an `optional<int>` constructed from `int*`). The narrowed `acc` (Optional -> T) assigned back into the Optional slot across the resumable frame is the trigger. No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error only. **Blocks `itertools.accumulate`** (the generic running-fold shape). Workaround: none in the generic generator form. Surfaced probing itertools v2 feasibility. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] A function/method that returns a recursive-union alias referenced *qualified* (`json.JsonValue`) fails to type-check (`expected JsonValue, got JsonValue`); the *unqualified* import (`from json import JsonValue`) compiles.** `import json; def p(s: str) -> json.JsonValue: return json.loads(s)` (and the `Own[json.JsonValue]` form, and the method form) is rejected -- the qualified alias resolves to a recursive-union form that does not match `json.loads`'s own return form, even though both print as `JsonValue`. `from json import loads, JsonValue` + `-> Own[JsonValue]` works. Almost certainly the recursive-union borrow/storage-form duality (OQ9): the cross-module qualified-alias reference produces a different form than the defining module's. Toolchain... actually a *sema* error, not silent. Workaround: import the alias by name (used by `tplib.requests.Response.json`). Reproducers `/tmp/agents/req/{m2,g1}.py`. Surfaced building `tplib.requests`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED] `isinstance`-narrowing a recursive-union element *extracted* from a container fails the C++ build unless the element is first bound to an explicitly-annotated local.** `d = json.loads(s); if isinstance(d, dict): v = d["k"]; if isinstance(v, int): ...` -> g++ `no matching function for call to holds_alternative<tpy::BigInt>(JsonValue&)` -- the extracted element is a *borrow* form (`JsonValue&`) on which `holds_alternative` is not callable. Binding `v: JsonValue = d["k"]` first (forcing a storage-form copy) makes the narrow compile and run. Shallow narrowing of the `loads` root (`isinstance(d, dict)`) is unaffected. Borrow/storage-form duality (OQ9) at the element-access boundary. Toolchain-caught, not silent. Workaround: explicit `: JsonValue` local (documented in `tplib.requests` -- affects every consumer of `Response.json()`). Reproducers `/tmp/agents/req/{g2,h2}.py`. Surfaced building `tplib.requests`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] For-iterating a narrowed `Optional[list]` accessed through an *attribute* emits a double-deref and fails the C++ build.** `if args.header is not None: for h in args.header: ...` (where `args.header: list[str] | None`, e.g. an argparse `action="append"` result) emits `auto& __obj_0 = (*(*args.header));` -- g++ `no match for operator* (operand type is std::vector<...>)`. The narrowing of the attribute does not carry to the for-loop's iterable lowering, which then derefs an already-deref'd value. *Subscripting* the same narrowed attribute works (`args.tag[0]` in `tests/cases/argparse/list_and_const_actions`), so the gap is specific to for-iteration of an Optional-list *attribute*. Binding to a local first (`hl = args.header; if hl is not None: for h in hl: ...`) narrows correctly and compiles -- used in `examples/net/curl.py`. Toolchain-caught, not silent. Sibling of the narrowed-Optional-dict key-iter entry above. Surfaced building the curl example on `tplib.requests`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] An `@overload`-ed generator METHOD is rejected at the stub: `Protocol type 'Iterator' cannot be used as a return type`.** `class C: @overload def rep[T](self, obj: T) -> Iterator[T]: ...` + a second stub + a `yield`-bodied implementation errors at the first stub's `def` line. Root: the `...`-bodied stub has `is_generator=False` (no `yield` in its body), and the method-registration return-type validation (`tpyc/sema/registration.py:1258`) rejects an `Iterator[T]` return unless `method.is_generator` -- whereas the free-function overload path (`register_overload_group`) does no protocol-return check on stubs at all, so it is lenient. Distinct from the free-function overloaded-generator crash (now fixed: the impl's `generator_yield_type` is set via `_set_generator_yield_type`); the method analog fails earlier and never reaches that path. The free-function form is the common one (itertools uses free functions), so this is lower priority. Fix shape: in the method return-type validation, treat an `Iterator[T]`-returning `@overload` stub whose group has a generator implementation as a generator (or relax the protocol-return check for overload stubs, mirroring the free-function path), then set the impl method's `generator_yield_type` (same `_set_generator_yield_type` helper). Surfaced by /tpy-fix-bug of the free-function overloaded generator. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] An annotated dict/list literal whose VALUES are container literals is rejected: `Type mismatch in variable 'g': expected list[Int32], got PendingList[Int32, 2]#0`.** `g: dict[str, list[Int32]] = {"a": [1, 2], "b": [3]}` fails, and so does the list flavor `m: list[list[Int32]] = [[1], [2, 3]]`. The annotation's element type never reaches the NESTED literal, so each inner literal stays a `PendingListType` and the outer coercion compares it against the resolved `list[Int32]` slot (`_analyze_var_decl` -> `compat.coerce_expr`, `tpyc/sema/statements.py:4196`). The named-local workaround compiles (`row: list[Int32] = [1, 2]; g = {"a": row}`). This is the sibling BUGS entry below already names as "the annotated dict-literal-of-list-literals case" -- it had no entry of its own. Loud reject-valid, no miscompile. Fix shape: thread the annotated container's element/value type into nested container literals during literal resolution, the same expected-type-into-nested-literal hole as the `d.get(k, [])` default. Repro `/tmp/agents/d2dbg/x/main.py`. Surfaced writing the value-position container-element exec case. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] `d.get(k, [])` (empty-list / collection-literal default) fails to compile: the literal default arg never resolves its element type.** `d: dict[str, list[Int32]]; d.get("k", [])` -> `No matching overload for 'get' with argument types (str, PendingList[???, 0])` -- the `[]` stays a `PendingListType` (no element-type context flows from the `default: V` param to the literal), so overload resolution can't match `get(key, default: V)`. The named-local workaround (`fb: list[Int32] = []; d.get(k, fb)`) compiles. Same expected-type-into-nested-literal hole as the annotated dict-literal-of-list-literals case (audit cluster 14 family); the `default` param's `V` should hint the literal. Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/getb/absent_rvalue.py`. Blocks the rvalue-default path of the dict.get(k,default) aliasing work (Stage B). Surfaced reproducing that work.
- **[LOW small] The F1 borrow-local const rule may emit `const T*` for a mutable borrow when a `@readonly` `@native` record method returns a reference type.** Now that native `-> V` reference returns alias (the native-record exclusion was removed), the readonly-method ref-return arm of `_f1_is_const` (`tpyc/thir/lower/predicates.py:7772`, the `isinstance(stmt.init, TpyMethodCall)` branch keyed on `fi.is_readonly and call_returns_cpp_ref(...)`) fires and renders the bound local `const T*`; if such a method intentionally exposes a mutable `T&` and the caller wants a mutable `T*`, the borrow is silently over-constrained. No current stdlib case (the affected methods -- e.g. uninit `load` -- pick the non-const C++ overload on a non-const receiver, and `const T*` from a mutable `T&` is a safe narrowing). Latent trap for future native bindings; confirmed by reading the surviving arm, not by a reproducer. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness).
- **[LOW small] `@cpp_template` accessor methods on `@native` containers (`list`/`Span`/`Array`/`varargs.unchecked_get`) now alias for reference-type element instantiations, untested.** The native-record exclusion removal generalized aliasing to all native `-> V` reference returns, including `@cpp_template` `operator[]`-style accessors; the `unchecked_get` family is exercised only for value-type elements, so the reference-element aliasing path (`list[SomeRecord].unchecked_get(i)` bound and mutated through) has no regression test. Behavior is believed correct (operator[] returns `T&`); the gap is coverage. Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness).
- **[LOW small] Free `@native` functions returning a bare reference type `-> V` value-copy the result where a `V&`-returning C++ function should alias.** `call_returns_cpp_ref` (`tpyc/value_category.py`) bails out for `is_native_import` (free native functions) before the `-> V` vs `-> Own[V]` return-shape check that now governs both user methods and `@native` *record* methods (the native-record exclusion was removed). So a free `@native` func whose hand-written C++ returns `V&` into an argument has its result copied at the call site, not aliased -- the same asymmetry the record-method fix closed, one layer up. Latent: no in-tree free native function currently returns a bare reference `-> V` (they return values, `Own`, `Optional`, or views). Fix: drop the remaining `fi.is_native_import and not fi.is_method` guard in `call_returns_cpp_ref` (the method half is already handled) so free functions also reach the return-shape check, after auditing free native bindings the way the record-method bindings were audited (confirm each bare-`-> V` free function actually returns `V&`, retype by-value ones to `-> Own[V]`). Surfaced removing the native-record return-convention exclusion.
- **[MED medium] Two-arg `dict.get(k, default)` returns a copy of the stored value where CPython returns the stored object -- warned, not yet aliased.** The dict-accessor aliasing work (audit cluster 7) made `items()`/`values()`/`setdefault()` borrow, but two-arg `get` stayed by-value: its result conditionally borrows EITHER the map slot (hit) OR the default argument (miss), and an rvalue default needs a materialization slot whose lifetime is unresolved for loops (per-iteration freshness vs slot reuse) and resumable frames (suspension-crossing borrows). Loud since the same work: a call-site warning fires for reference-type values, silenced by wrapping in `copy()`; value-type results are parity-clean. Fix shape: `V& dict_get_default(m&, key, V& def)` + const overload (value-type V keeps the by-value helper, dispatched by codegen), an emit-site slot for rvalue defaults with defined loop/suspension semantics, and `return_borrows_from={-1, default}` so borrow tracking roots at both sources; typing the return as a bare `-> V` (not `Own[V]`) then makes the result alias with no extra mechanism (the precedent: setdefault is a plain `-> V` native method that aliases because native `-> V` reference returns are treated as `T&`), and the `@copy_returns_warn` decorator is dropped from the overload at the same time (the warning becomes unnecessary once the result aliases). Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A pending dict/set LOCAL passed to a param with a wider value/element type is rejected instead of widening (`{"a": 1}` local into `dict[str, Int64]` param -> "expected Int64, got Int32").** Symmetric everywhere (free functions, methods, ctors) -- `mark_container_param_context`'s dict/set arms only call `_widen_inferred_type`, which records the widening for the literal's storage but the arg-check still compares the pre-widening pending type against the param and errors. The LIST arm handles this (`coerced_element_type` makes `xs = [3]; take(xs)` into `list[Int64]` compile), so the gap is dict/set parity with the list behavior. Loud reject-valid, trivial workaround (annotate the local). Reproducer: `/tmp/agents/setbug/dictwiden.py`. Surfaced authoring the pending-arg-marks tests. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A *simple* generator (single yield in a tail for-loop) iterating a *temporary* generator source emits an undeclared-temporary capture.** `def passthrough(n): for x in gen_repeat(5, n): yield x` (where `gen_repeat` is a generator, so `gen_repeat(5, n)` is a temporary) -> g++ `'__tmp_1' was not declared in this scope`: the peephole lambda capture spells `__src = std::optional<std::decay_t<decltype(gen_repeat<int32_t>(__tmp_1, n))>>()` referencing a `__tmp_1` that is never declared in the lambda's scope. Pre-existing (reproduces without the self-iterator-copy fix); confined to the simple-generator make_generator peephole over a temporary call source. The *resumable* path (multi-yield, or break/continue) handles this correctly. No silent miscompile -- C++ build error. Workaround: bind the source first (`g = gen_repeat(5, n); for x in g: ...`), or make the consumer resumable. Fix shape: the peephole must materialize the temporary source arg before the lambda capture (or stash it like the resumable `__for_src`). Surfaced authoring the resumable self-iterator-copy fix's inverse tests. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small]** Async finally-with-await (CFG-based finally) is silently skipped when the coroutine frame is dropped mid-suspension WITHOUT cancellation (a frame abandoned outside the executor's cancel-drain path). The frame destructor runs helper-based finallies and `with.__exit__`s, but a finally body that itself suspends cannot run in a destructor. The generator sibling (yield-in-finally) gets a compile-time warning; the async shape does not, because the normal executor path runs such cleanup via cancellation (CancelledError at the suspension) and a blanket warning would flag every legitimate `finally: await ...`. Fix shape: warn only for frames that can escape executor-managed lifetime, or drain-to-completion in the owning slot before drop. CPython runs the finally at GC close.
- **[LOW small]** An `except BaseException:` (or `except GeneratorExit:`) handler around a `yield` does not observe the close when the generator is abandoned: CPython throws GeneratorExit INTO the frame, so such a handler catches it and its body runs; TPy's frame destructor runs only pending finally helpers and `with.__exit__`s (it cannot resume arbitrary handler code inside a destructor), so the handler body is skipped silently. Same can't-resume-in-a-destructor family as the warned yield-in-finally skip, but no diagnostic fires for the handler shape. Fix shape: extend the yield-in-finally warning to yields lexically inside an except-BaseException/GeneratorExit-guarded try, or accept and document. Surfaced by the GeneratorExit-on-close design pass.
- **[LOW small]** `break`/`continue` crossing a CFG-based finally (finally body contains a suspension) silently skips that finally body: `CFGBuilder._build_break/_build_continue` emit a plain Fall to the loop's break/continue BB without routing through `finally_entry_bb` (returns are parked via the pending-return slot; break/continue have no analogous path). Same hole for break inside an except handler of such a try (`ExceptRegion.parent_finally_entry_bb`). Repro in the 2026-06-10 audit (B62): async `for` + `try/finally`-with-await + `break` drops `cleanup 1`; the generator shape shares the emitter. Fix shape: park a pending-jump target the way pending returns are parked. Helper-based finallies are unaffected.
- **[LOW small] An explicitly-annotated `Array[T, N]` comprehension rejected by the stack-build gates fails with a misleading generic type mismatch.** `xs: Array[Int32, 2000] = [i for i in range(2000)]` (over the `_COMP_ARRAY_MAX_SIZE` cap) and `xs: Array[Int32, 4] = [g(i) for i in range(4)]` with `@error_return` `g` inside try/except both error with "expected Array[...], got list[...]" -- the gates in `_try_comp_array_size` (`tpyc/sema/expressions.py`) suppress the PendingListType machinery entirely, so the explicit-annotation resolution rule never runs; both shapes compiled at the pre-builder base via the old loop build. Loud rejection, not a miscompile, but it rejects previously-valid code with a diagnostic that doesn't name the cause. Fix shape needs a design call: either honor the annotation with a non-lambda build for gated shapes (the loop-fill reintroduces the default-ctor side-effect divergence the builder fixed, so only sound where construction is side-effect-free) or emit a targeted error ("cannot stack-build: element calls @error_return / size exceeds cap") at the annotation-mismatch site. Surfaced by the /tpy-ready retrospective challenger.
- **[LOW small] Reading an `@error_return` property outside try/except is not rejected; the same call spelled as a method is.** The unhandled-error_return check (`tpyc/sema/calls.py:4706`) fires for direct and method calls but not for the getter hidden behind a property read: with `@property @error_return(E) def val(...)`, a bare `g.scaled(1)` outside try/except errors with "must be handled with try/except" while the adjacent `g.val` compiles and the unwrap panics at runtime on error instead. Missing safety diagnostic, not a miscompile (codegen's panic fallback is sound). Fix: run the unhandled check on the sema-attached `property_getter_call` like any other resolved call. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the index-sequence builder (the gate-test regeneration flagged only the method line).
- **[LOW small] Repeating a mutable reference-type element has no "copies" diagnostic, asymmetric with the bulk-copy warning.** `[obj] * N` evaluates the element once and copies it into every slot where CPython aliases the same object N times -- mutating `xs[0]` updates all CPython views but only one TPy copy. The divergence is declared in `docs/LANGUAGE_FEATURES.md` (list repetition) but emits no compile-time signal, while the sibling bulk-copy path (`list(b)` over reference elements) warns "copies X elements" with `copy_iter()` as the acknowledgment spelling (`tpyc/sema/calls.py`). Pre-existing for the vector repeat path; the Array repeat path now shares it. Fix shape (design-gated: new warning + acknowledgment spelling need sign-off): warn on repeating a mutable reference-type element, silenced by an explicit per-slot construction or an acknowledgment spelling consistent with `copy_iter`. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the repeat-pair fix.
- **[LOW small] A comprehension whose element is a reference-typed field access (`[obj.ref_field for obj in src]`) fails the C++ build with "forming pointer to reference type".** `[b.inner for b in bs]` where `Box.inner: Inner` (a reference-type field) and `bs: list[Box]` emits a `std::vector<Inner>` build that g++ rejects (`forming pointer to reference type 'Inner&'` inside `allocator`/`construct_at`). Pre-existing and independent of the source's ownership -- reproduces identically over a borrowed `list` source and an `Own[T]`-yielding generator. The comprehension element binds the field access as `Inner&` and the storage-form result vector mis-forms a pointer to it. Loud build error, not a miscompile. Workaround: bind the field to a local first (`[copy(b.inner) for b in bs]` or an explicit loop). Surfaced building a derived-sink test case for the list/set comprehension-element move fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] (rejects-valid, loud) A generator *expression* whose source is a CALL is a hard compile error, though list/set/dict comprehensions over the same source work.** `sum(x for x in two_then(3))` (where `two_then` is a resumable generator) -> `error: in function 'main': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (genexpr.iterable_shape)`; the same genexpr over an ordinary `Own[list[Int32]]`-returning call reports `(expr.genexpr)` at the outer gate. `_lower_genexpr` (`tpyc/thir/lower/comprehensions.py`, ~1169-1202) admits only a `range()` source, a bare-name lvalue `list`/`set`/`Array`/`Span`, or a container literal; every other iterable -- any call, and `dict` -- raises `ThirUnsupported("genexpr.iterable_shape")`. The list/set/dict comprehension form over the identical generator still compiles (verified), so the underlying iteration render is fine and only the genexpr admission gate is narrow. EVERYDAY shape (a genexpr over any function call), worth queueing. Fix shape: give the genexpr path the same primed begin()/end() driving the comprehension uses. Workaround: use a list/set/dict comprehension, or materialize via `list(...)`. Surfaced building the itertools stdlib module. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, diagnostics] Growing an inferred fixed-`Array` sublist via the outer subscript surfaces a raw g++ error, not a TPy diagnostic.** `rows = [[i, i + 1] for i in range(3)]; rows[0].append(99)` -- the inner literal `[i, i+1]` is constant-size and unmutated, so it resolves to `std::array<int32_t, 2>` (the stack-Array optimization), and `rows[0].append(...)` then fails the C++ build with `'std::array<int, 2>' has no member named 'push_back'`. Mutation *through the outer subscript* is not tracked back to the inner literal, so the inner is never promoted to `list`. Loud failure, not a miscompile; the workaround is an explicit `rows: list[list[int]] = [...]` (forces `vector<vector<...>>`, append works -- covered by `tests/cases/list/comp_nested_vector_inner`). A leaky-C++-error class (raw g++ message instead of a TPy diagnostic). The uniform outer/middle levels of a deep-nested literal (e.g. `[[[1, 2], [3, 4]], [[5, 6], [7, 8]]]`) are another way to reach it: those levels stay fixed `Array`, so `xs.append(...)` / `xs[0].append(...)` on them hits the same raw g++ error. Fix shape: either detect element-mutation through a container subscript and promote the inner pending list to `list`, or emit a TPy diagnostic at the `.append` site pointing at the `list[list[T]]` annotation. The fix's regression test (a now-rejected-with-clean-message `error_` case, or a happy case once promotion lands) goes in with the fix. Surfaced while finishing the nested-list-literal work. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small, diagnostics] Pending container type names leak into type-mismatch / unresolved-type diagnostics** (`PendingList[Int32, 2]#0`, `PendingDict[...]#1`). User-facing errors expose the internal deferred-resolution representation instead of a resolved display name (`list[int]`, etc.); the `error_append_incompatible_nested` and `error_jagged_incompatible_elem` cases show both sides of a mismatch as raw `PendingList[...]`. Worse, the mixed-types error's *suggested fix* embeds the same repr -- `Use a type annotation like list[PendingList[Int32, 2]#0 | PendingList[str, 3]#1]` -- which is unwritable (a user can't type `#0`), so the suggestion is useless until the names resolve. Pre-existing, cross-cutting all pending-type errors. Fix shape: a `PendingList`/`PendingDict`/`PendingSet` -> resolved-display-name helper (defer to the inferred element type) applied at the diagnostic-formatting boundary, *including the suggested-annotation string* (which then reads `list[list[int] | list[str]]`). Surfaced by /tpy-review (codegen-correctness) of the pending-container-compat fix; suggestion face flagged reviewing the jagged-nested-list diagnostics. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] A dict comprehension evaluates the key and value in unspecified order (CPython evaluates the key first), observable only with ordering-dependent side effects.** `{f(): g() for _ in it}` emits `__result.insert_or_assign(f(), g())` -- C++ leaves the two argument evaluations unsequenced, so `g()` may run before `f()`, whereas CPython's bytecode evaluates the key expression before the value. Pure/side-effect-free key/value (the overwhelming common case) are unaffected; only a key and value with a mutual ordering dependence (e.g. both mutate a shared counter) diverge. The owned-value-move path already sequences the key into a local before the value move (`{ auto __k = key; insert_or_assign(std::move(__k), std::move(value)); }`), so it is key-before-value correct; only the non-owned/non-moving path stays unsequenced. **Fix shape:** sequence the key into a local for the non-owned path too (or whenever either side may have side effects). Pre-existing; surfaced by /tpy-review (cpython-parity) of the dict comprehension owned-element move. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW] (rejects-valid, loud) A mixed-arm ternary (`g0 if cond else C(9)`) of a reference type is a hard compile error.** When one arm is a reference lvalue and the other a fresh rvalue, sema first warns "ternary copies a reference type where CPython would alias the variable arm; use copy() to acknowledge the copy" (`tpyc/sema/statements.py:3919-3923`, keyed on `is_rvalue_source` in `tpyc/value_category.py`, which uses OR semantics over the arms so a fresh arm forces materialization), and then codegen refuses the shape outright: in a local-decl slot `error: in function 'main': this construct is not yet supported by C++ code generation (stmt.var_decl:decl.slot_type)` (raised at `tpyc/thir/lower/statements.py:9978`), and in an argument slot `(stmt.expr_stmt:call.arg_shape.record_f1)`. So the silent value-vs-reference divergence this entry was filed for is no longer reachable -- valid Python is refused loudly instead. The all-lvalue-arms ternary (`g0 if cond else g1`) still compiles and aliases correctly, so binding the fresh arm to a local first is a verified workaround. **Fix shape:** materialize both arms into a common borrow (e.g. a pointer-of-the-selected-arm) rather than a value, weighed against the cost of the extra indirection. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] Annotated assignment to an attribute (`self.vals: list[Int32] = [5]` in `__init__`) is rejected with `error: Invalid assignment target`.** CPython accepts annotated attribute targets (PEP 526); this is the idiomatic way to declare-and-init instance fields in `__init__`, so plain Python sources hit it immediately. The unannotated form (`self.vals = [5]`) plus a class-level annotation works, so the workaround is trivial, but the diagnostic does not say that. **Fix shape:** either accept the annotated form (treat the annotation as the field declaration, mirroring the class-level path) or reject with a targeted message pointing at the class-level-annotation convention. Surfaced writing repros for audit item #5. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The "copies X into owned storage" warning renders unresolved internal type names for list-literal locals.** When the copied variable is an unannotated list literal, the warning prints the pre-resolution placeholder -- `copies PendingList[IntLiteral(1), 3]#1 into owned storage` -- because the coercion-path warning fires during body analysis, before container-literal resolution picks the final `list[T]`/`Array[T, N]` type. - **[MED small] (rejects valid code) Sema types an `as` over an or-group as the FULL subject and requires or-pattern alternatives to bind IDENTICAL types, so an `as` on a multi-class or-pattern of a union subject cannot be written at all.** [`or-pattern-as-binding-no-join`] Two halves of one rule. First, `case (Dog() | Cat()) as y:` on `Dog | Cat | Bird` binds `y` as `Bird | Cat | Dog` rather than `Dog | Cat` -- every non-class `as` inner falls to `bindings[name] = subject_type` in `tpyc/sema/match.py`, so `y.n` is rejected even when every alternative has the field. Second, `_analyze_or_pattern` raises `variable 'y' has type 'Dog' in first alternative but 'Cat' in another` whenever alternatives disagree, so the per-alternative spelling `case (Dog() as y) | (Cat() as y):` and the nested `case ((Dog() | Cat()) as y) | (Bird() as y):` (pinned as-is by `tests/cases/match/error_or_nested_as_binds_wide`) are refused outright. CPython binds `y` to the matched object in every one of these. TPy has a well-formed type for it: the JOIN of the alternatives' binding types (a union, the subject's own type in the widest case), which is what the borrow-form variant already carries. Fix shape: an `as` over an or-group binds the union of its alternatives' resolved types, and `_analyze_or_pattern` joins per-name types across alternatives instead of demanding equality (the name-set check stays strict). Sema-side twin of the dropped-emit trio directly above (Optional / union / record); land them as ONE unit, since fixing the typing alone flips those loud C++ errors into silent stale-value reads for pre-declared names. The June audit recorded the typing half with this fix direction and it never reached this file. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED small] (rejects valid code) `case A() | None:` on a nullable union subject is rejected, though `case None:` alone dispatches on the same variant index the or-group would need.** [`or-pattern-none-alt-union`] `match v:` over `A | B | None` with `case A() | None:` errors `unsupported alternative in an or-pattern over a union subject; every alternative must name a union member class -- give 'None' or a literal its own 'case' arm` from `_check_union_or_alternatives` in `tpyc/sema/match.py:1562` (pinned as-is by `tests/cases/match/error_or_union_none_alt`). The rejection's stated reason -- that `None` names no member class so there is no label to emit -- is wrong for `None`: both union tiers already emit a `None` arm as a numeric `case <idx>:` off `_union_member_index(members, NoneType())` (`tpyc/thir/lower/match.py:3026` and `:3139`, scanning the member order `_union_index_members` builds at `:201`), so stacking that label under the class labels of the same group is the whole fix for the None alternative, with the as-binding (BUGS.md#or-pattern-as-binding-no-join) being the only interaction to think about. A LITERAL alternative on a union carrying a value member (`case A() | 5:` on `A | Int32`) is the genuinely unimplemented half: it needs the value member's index plus an `==` on the payload, i.e. the guarded tier's shape. Split the diagnostic accordingly -- accept `None`, and report a literal as not-yet-implemented rather than as a rule. CPython matches both. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.

Without a field condition the guard may read the capture. The older symptom was ill-formed C++ -- the composed `if (__case_1.legs == 4 && (n == "rex"))` preceded the `auto& n = __case_1.name;` declaration -- so it was loud either way; it is now caught in the front end instead of by the toolchain. CPython evaluates the guard after all pattern bindings, so the correct emit is bindings-then-nested-guard (`if (conds) { bindings; if (guard) ... }`), which is also the shape the record tier already uses. Worth queueing -- a field literal plus a named capture in one pattern is an everyday `match`. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED, deferred: MIR] Reading / narrowing the UNION ELEMENT of a borrow-form tuple fails the C++ build.** `def f(pair: tuple[Dog | Cat, Int32]): e = pair[0]; if isinstance(e, Dog): return e.bark` -- binding the union element to a local emits `std::variant<Cat*, Dog*> e = ::tpy::to_ptr_variant(std::get<0>(pair))`, wrong twice: in a borrow-form tuple the element is ALREADY a (const) pointer variant `variant<const Cat*, const Dog*>`, so `to_ptr_variant` (which expects a storage variant) is the wrong helper, and the local `e` is typed with mutable pointees that don't match the const source. The tuple-element read reuses the union-FIELD read path (storage -> pointer lift) instead of recognizing the borrow-tuple element is pointer-form already. No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error only. The boundary conversion (passing a `tuple[A|B,...]`, reading non-union elements, param->param passthrough) now works -- only extracting/narrowing the union element itself is broken. **Fix shape:** a union element read from a borrow-form tuple is already pointer-form -- bind the local to the element's const pointer-variant directly (no `to_ptr_variant` lift), and type the local to match (const pointees). Distinct mechanism from the boundary borrow-conversion (subscript read + `ptr_variant_locals` tracking + narrowing). Surfaced by /tpy-fix-bug of the union-tuple-element boundary fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[MED, deferred: MIR] The storage / local / field directions of a union tuple element are not wired (only the param/return/passthrough boundary works).** `TupleType._element_is_pointer_repr` (`tpyc/typesys.py`) deliberately EXCLUDES `UnionType`, so `has_pointer_repr_element()` is False for a union-only / union+value tuple -- the storage<->borrow wrap sites (`tuple_to_storage` / `tuple_to_pointer`) never fire for it, and a union-element tuple bound to a local from a storage source, stored in a record field / container, or moved as `Own[tuple[...]]` is not converted between the value-variant storage form and the pointer-variant borrow form. The boundary case works through a different path (`UnionType.to_cpp_return` for the param/return signature + `borrow_value_elem` for the rvalue call-arg, neither gated on `has_pointer_repr_element`). Also unwired: `readonly[tuple[A|B,...]]` params and nullable union elements (`tuple[A|B|None,...]`) beyond the boundary. No TPy diagnostic; C++ build error (or silent miss) only. **Fix shape:** the missing half is the gate -- extend `_element_is_pointer_repr` (and the per-element tuple storage/borrow converters in `runtime/cpp/include/tpy/format.hpp`) to route union elements through `to_ptr_variant`/`to_const_ptr_variant`/`to_value_variant`, with a const-aware (copy, not move) borrow->storage path since a union tuple element is always a const borrow. Related to the union-element extraction entry above and the recursive-wrapper-element exclusion below. Surfaced by /tpy-review of the union-tuple-element boundary fix. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug` (or `/tpy-add-feature`).
- **[LOW] An inherited async construct is rejected when the coro-struct owner's type args are not concretely bound (not yet supported).** Two triggers, same root cause: (a) a MULTI-LEVEL chain -- `class C(B[Int32])` where `B[U](A[U])` and `A[T]` defines `async def fetch(self) -> T`; (b) a GENERIC subclass of a generic base instantiated concretely -- `class Child[U](Box[U])` then `Child[Int32](...)`. In both, `await c.fetch()` (or inherited `async with` / `async for`) is rejected with a clear diagnostic ("multi-level generic inheritance chain is not yet supported") rather than miscompiled. Root cause: `RecordInfo.mro_ancestors` (`compute_mro_ancestors`, `tpyc/typesys.py`) records each base with the *defining* class's own type params, not the receiver's instantiation -- `C.mro_ancestors` holds `A[U]`, and `Child.mro_ancestors` holds `Box[U]` (U unbound) -- so the coro-struct owner carries an unbound `TypeParamRef`, which codegen cannot spell. Async-only: coro-struct naming is the one path that reads ancestor type args off `mro_ancestors` directly; sync method resolution / field access substitute via the *receiver's* own `type_args` and are unaffected (a sync inherited method on `Child[U](Box[U])` instantiated concretely works correctly). The direct single-level case (`IntBox(Box[Int32])` -- a *non-generic* subclass) also works. **Fix shape:** thread the receiver's instantiation args (and each intermediate level's args) into the `mro_ancestors` binding so ancestor type params resolve to concrete args, then drop the codegen guard in `gen_async.py::_sub_struct_qualname`. Surfaced by /tpy-fix-bug of the single-level generic-base inherited-async fix.
- **[LOW small] `with` / `async with` / `async for` walk the MRO for their dunders, but subscript (`__getitem__` / `__setitem__`) lookup does not.** A subclass that inherits `__getitem__` / `__setitem__` from a base (without overriding) silently fails the subscript operator -- the slice-lookup sites in `tpyc/sema/expressions.py` (`record.methods.get("__getitem__")` / `"__setitem__"`, ~lines 3479/3520) are own-only, unlike the MRO-aware `get_method_overloads_with_parents` now used for the with/async-with/async-for manager/iterator dunders. Pre-existing (present on master); same inherited-dunder gap, different operator. **Fix shape:** route the subscript dunder lookups through `get_method_overloads_with_parents` too. Surfaced by /tpy-review (architecture-fit) of the inherited-async fix.
- **[LOW small] A generic record's type-parameter bound is not enforced at a bare annotation that does not construct.** `x: Box[Rc[Int32]]` where `class Box[T: Send]` is accepted with no error even though `Rc[Int32]` violates the `T: Send` bound -- `tpyc/sema/type_ops.py::validate_record_type_args` (reached from variable-annotation validation) checks arity / kind / forward-refs but never consults `record_info.type_param_bounds` via `satisfies_bound`. Construction sites DO enforce it (`_analyze_record_constructor` in `calls.py`, and the generic-factory call path), so a record obtainable only via a constructor/factory (e.g. `Channel` via `channel[T: Send]()`) is covered in practice; the gap is bare annotations with no construction. Surfaced designing `Channel[T]` Send enforcement (Phase 4); applies directly to the channel's `Sender`/`Receiver`/`_ChanState` records (which now carry the `T: Send` bound) -- e.g. `rx: Receiver[SharedCache]` as a bare annotation is not rejected, only `channel[SharedCache](...)` at construction is. **Fix shape:** have `validate_record_type_args` validate substituted type args against the record's `type_param_bounds` via `satisfies_bound`, mirroring the construction-site check. Needs `/tpy-fix-bug`.
- **[LOW small] The `Iterable[Own[T]]` copy-warning suppression is position-agnostic, silently dropping a legitimate warning for multi-arg containers.** The conformance check (`tpyc/sema/compatibility.py`, `actual_provides_own`) suppresses the "copies T elements; use copy_iter()" warning whenever the actual type carries `Own` in ANY type-arg slot.
